entries.860b379fcdbaa1e3fc2c88b36d12e2075cf43b1f: <div sID="gen15969" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="Isa.24" sID="Isa.24"/> <div eID="gen15969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15970" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15971" type="x-p"/> It is agreed that here begins a new sermon, which is continued to the end of <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1-Isa.27.13">chap. xxvii.</reference> And in it the prophet, according to the directions he had received, does, in many precious promises, "say to the righteous, It shall be well with them;" and, in many dreadful threatenings, he says, "Woe to the wicked, it shall be ill with them" (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.10-Isa.3.11">ch. iii. 10, 11</reference>); and these are interwoven, that they may illustrate each other. This chapter is mostly threatening; and, as the judgments threatened are very sore and grievous ones, so the people threatened with those judgments are very many. It is not the burden of any particular city or kingdom, as those before, but the burden of the whole earth. The word indeed signifies only the land, because our own land is commonly to us as all the earth. But it is here explained by another word that is not so confined; it is the world (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.4">ver. 4</reference>); so that it must at least take in a whole neighbourhood of nations. 1. Some think (and very probably) that it is a prophecy of the great havoc that Sennacherib and his Assyrian army should now shortly make of many of the nations in that part of the world. 2. Others make it to point at the like devastations which, about 100 years afterwards, Nebuchadnezzar and his armies should make in the same countries, going from one kingdom to another, not only to conquer them, but to ruin them and lay them waste; for that was the method which those eastern nations took in their wars. The promises that are mixed with the threatenings are intended for the support and comfort of the people of God in those very calamitous times. And, since here are no particular nations names either by whom or on whom those desolations should be brought, I see not but it may refer to both these events. Nay, the scripture has many fulfillings, and we ought to give it its full latitude; and therefore I incline to think that the prophet, from those and the like instances which he had a particular eye to, designs here to represent in general the calamitous state of mankind, and the many miseries which human life is liable to, especially those that attend the wars of the nations. Surely the prophets were sent, not only to foretel particular events, but to form the minds of men to virtue and piety, and for that end their prophecies were written and preserved even for our learning, and therefore ought not to be looked upon as of private interpretation. Now since a thorough conviction of the vanity of the world, and its insufficiency to make us happy, will go far towards bringing us to God, and drawing out our affections towards another world, the prophet here shows what vexation of spirit we must expect to meet with in these things, that we may never take up our rest in them, nor promise ourselves satisfaction any where short of the enjoyment of God. In this chapter we have, I. A threatening of desolating judgments for sin (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.1-Isa.24.12">ver. 1-12</reference>), to which is added an assurance that in the midst of them good people should be comforted, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.13-Isa.24.15">ver. 13-15</reference>. II. A further threatening of the like desolations (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.16-Isa.24.22">ver. 16-22</reference>), to which is added an assurance that in the midst of all God should be glorified.
entries.2d6b92a4c43bab2563184616a900da74acf618e8: <div eID="gen15971" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15970" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">General Desolation Announced. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 718.)</title> <div sID="gen15972" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him. <hi type="super">3</hi> The land shall be utterly emptied, and utterly spoiled: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken this word. <hi type="super">4</hi> The earth mourneth <hi type="italic">and</hi> fadeth away, the world languisheth <hi type="italic">and</hi> fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish. <hi type="super">5</hi> The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant. <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore hath the curse devoured the earth, and they that dwell therein are desolate: therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men left. <hi type="super">7</hi> The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, all the merry-hearted do sigh. <hi type="super">8</hi> The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth. <hi type="super">9</hi> They shall not drink wine with a song; strong drink shall be bitter to them that drink it. <hi type="super">10</hi> The city of confusion is broken down: every house is shut up, that no man may come in. <hi type="super">11</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a crying for wine in the streets; all joy is darkened, the mirth of the land is gone. <hi type="super">12</hi> In the city is left desolation, and the gate is smitten with destruction. <div eID="gen15972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15973" type="x-p"/> It is a very dark and melancholy scene that this prophecy presents to our view; turn our eyes which way we will, every thing looks dismal. The threatened desolations are here described in a great variety of expressions to the same purport, and all aggravating. <div eID="gen15973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15974" type="x-p"/> I. The earth is stripped of all its ornaments and looks as if it were taken off its basis; it is made <hi type="italic">empty and waste</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">v. 1</reference>), as if it were reduced to its first chaos, <hi type="italic">Tohu</hi> and <hi type="italic">Bohu,</hi> nothing but confusion and emptiness again (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Gen. i. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">without form and void.</hi> It is true earth sometimes signifies the <hi type="italic">land,</hi> and so the same word <hi type="italic">eretz</hi> is here translated (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">The land shall be utterly emptied and utterly spoiled;</hi> but I see not why it should not there, as well as <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">v. 1</reference>, be translated <hi type="italic">the earth;</hi> for most commonly, if not always, where it signifies some one particular land it has something joined to it, or at least not far from it, which does so appropriate it; as the land (or earth) of Egypt, or Canaan, or this land, or ours, or yours, or the like. It might indeed refer to some particular country, and an ambiguous word might be used to warrant such an application; for it is good to apply to ourselves, and our own hands, what the scripture says in general of the vanity and vexation of spirit that attend all things here below; but it should seem designed to speak what often happens to many countries, and will do while the world stands, and what may, we know not how soon, happen to our own, and what is the general character of all earthly things: they are empty of all solid comfort and satisfaction; a little thing makes them waste. We often see numerous families, and plentiful estates, utterly emptied and utterly spoiled, by one judgment or other, or perhaps only by a gradual and insensible decay. Sin has turned the earth <hi type="italic">upside down;</hi> the earth has become quite a different thing to man from what it was when God made it to be his habitation. Sin has also <hi type="italic">scattered abroad the inhabitants thereof.</hi> The rebellion at Babel was the occasion of the dispersion there. How many ways are there in which the inhabitants both of towns and of private houses are scattered abroad, so that near relations and old neighbours know nothing of one another! To the same purport is <reference osisRef="Isa.24.4">v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">The earth mourns, and fades away;</hi> it disappoints those that placed their happiness in it and raised their expectations high from it, and proves not what they promised themselves it would be. <hi type="italic">The</hi> whole <hi type="italic">world languishes and fades away,</hi> as hastening towards a dissolution. It is, at the best, like a flower, which withers in the hands of those that please themselves too much with it, and lay it in their bosoms. And, as the earth itself grows old, so those that dwell therein are desolate; men carry crazy sickly bodies along with them, are often solitary, and confined by affliction, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.6">v. 6</reference>. When the earth languishes, and is not so fruitful as it used to be, then those that dwell therein, that make it their home, and rest, and portion, are desolate; whereas those that by faith dwell in God can rejoice in him even when the fir-tree does not blossom. If we look abroad, and see in how many places pestilences and burning fevers rage, and what multitudes are swept away by them in a little time, so that sometimes the living scarcely suffice to bury the dead, perhaps we shall understand what the prophet means when he says, <hi type="italic">The inhabitants of the earth are burned,</hi> or consumed, some by one disease, others by another, and there are but <hi type="italic">few men left,</hi> in comparison. Note, The world we live in is a world of disappointment, a vale of tears, and a dying world; and the children of men in it are but of few days, and full of trouble. <div eID="gen15974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15975" type="x-p"/> II. It is God that brings all these calamities upon the earth. <hi type="italic">The Lord</hi> that made the earth, and made it fruitful and beautiful, for the service and comfort of man, now <hi type="italic">makes it empty and waste</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">v. 1</reference>), for its Creator is and will be its Judge; he has an incontestable right to pass sentence upon it and an irresistible power to execute that sentence. It is <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> that <hi type="italic">has spoken this word,</hi> and he will do the work (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.3">v. 3</reference>); it is his curse that has <hi type="italic">devoured the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.6">v. 6</reference>), the general curse which sin brought upon <hi type="italic">the ground for man's sake</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.17">Gen. iii. 17</reference>), and all the particular curses which families and countries bring upon themselves by their enormous wickedness. See the power of God's curse, how it makes all empty and lays all waste; those whom he curses are cursed indeed. <div eID="gen15975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15976" type="x-p"/> III. Persons of all ranks and conditions shall share in these calamities (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">It shall be as with the people, so with the priest,</hi> &c. This is true of many of the common calamities of human life; all are subject to the same diseases of body, sorrows of mind, afflictions in relations, and the like. There is one event to those of very different stations; time and chance happen to them all. It is in a special manner true of the destroying judgments which God sometimes brings upon sinful nations; when he pleases he can make them universal, so that none shall escape them or be exempt from them; whether men have little or much, they shall lose it all. Those of the meaner rank smart first by famine; but those of the higher rank go first into captivity, while the poor of the land are left. It shall be all alike, 1. With high and low: <hi type="italic">As with the people, so with the priest,</hi> or prince. The dignity of magistrates and ministers, and the respect and reverence due to both, shall not secure them. <hi type="italic">The faces of elders are not honoured,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.5.12">Lam. v. 12</reference>. The priests had been as corrupt and wicked as the people; and, if their character served not to restrain them from sin, how can they expect it should serve to secure them from judgments? In both it is <hi type="italic">like people, like priest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.4.8-Hos.4.9">Hosea iv. 8, 9</reference>. 2. With bond and free: <hi type="italic">As with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress.</hi> They have all corrupted their way, and therefore will all be made miserable when the earth is made waste. 3. With rich and poor. Those that have money before-hand, that are purchasing, and letting out money to interest, will fare no better than those that are so impoverished that they are forced to sell their estates and take up money at interest. There are judgments short of the great day of judgment in which rich and poor meet together. Let not those that are advanced in the world set their inferiors at too great a distance, because they know not how soon they may be set upon a level with them. <hi type="italic">The rich man's wealth is his strong city</hi> in his own conceit; but it does not always prove so. <div eID="gen15976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15977" type="x-p"/> IV. It is sin that brings these calamities upon the earth. The earth is made empty, and fades away, because it <hi type="italic">is defiled under the inhabitants thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.5">v. 5</reference>); it is polluted by the sins of men, and therefore it is made desolate by the judgments of God. Such is the filthy nature of sin that it defiles the earth itself under the sinful inhabitants thereof, and it is rendered unpleasant in the eyes of God and good men. See <reference osisRef="Lev.18.25">Lev. xviii. 25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.27">27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.28">28</reference>. Blood, in particular, defiles the land, <reference osisRef="Num.35.33">Num. xxxv. 33</reference>. The earth never spues out its inhabitants till they have first defiled it by their sins. Why, what have they done? 1. They have transgressed the laws of their creation, not answered the ends of it. The bonds of the law of nature have been broken by them, and they have cast from them the cords of their obligations to the God of nature. 2. <hi type="italic">They have changed the ordinances</hi> of revealed religion, those of them that have had the benefit of that. <hi type="italic">They have neglected the ordinances</hi> (so some read it), and have made no conscience of observing them. They have passed over the laws, in the commission of sin, and have passed by the ordinance, in the omission of duty. 3. Herein they have <hi type="italic">broken the everlasting covenant,</hi> which is a perpetual bond and will be to those that keep it a perpetual blessing. It is God's wonderful condescension that he is pleased to deal with men in a covenant-way, to do them good, and thereby oblige them to do him service. Even those that had no benefit by God's covenant with Abraham had benefit by his covenant with Noah and his sons, which is called <hi type="italic">an everlasting covenant,</hi> his covenant with day and night; but they observe not the precepts of the sons of Noah, they acknowledge not God's goodness in the day and night, nor study to make him any grateful returns, and so break the everlasting covenant and defeat the gracious designs and intentions of it. <div eID="gen15977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15978" type="x-p"/> V. These judgments shall humble men's pride and mar their mirth. When the earth is made empty, 1. It is a great mortification to men's pride (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The haughty people of the earth do languish;</hi> for they have lost that which supported their pride, and for which they magnified themselves. As for those that have held their heads highest, God can make them hang the head. 2. It is a great damp to men's jollity. This is enlarged upon much (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.7-Isa.24.9">v. 7-9</reference>): <hi type="italic">All the merry-hearted do sigh.</hi> Such is the nature of carnal mirth, it is but <hi type="italic">as the crackling of thorns under a pot,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.6">Eccl. vii. 6</reference>. Great laughters commonly end in a sigh. Those that make the world their chief joy cannot rejoice ever more. When God sends his judgments into the earth he designs thereby to make those serious that were wholly addicted to their pleasures. <hi type="italic">Let your laughter be turned into mourning.</hi> When the earth is emptied the <hi type="italic">noise of those that rejoice in it ends.</hi> Carnal joy is a noisy thing; but the noise of it will soon be at an end, and the end of it is heaviness. Two things are made use of to excite and express vain mirth, and the jovial crew is here deprived of both:—(1.) Drinking: <hi type="italic">The new wine mourns;</hi> it has grown sour for want of drinking; for, how proper soever it may be for the heavy heart (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.6">Prov. xxxi. 6</reference>), it does not relish to them as it does to the merry-hearted. <hi type="italic">The vine languishes,</hi> and gives little hopes of a vintage, and therefore <hi type="italic">the merry-hearted do sigh;</hi> for they know no other gladness than that of their corn, and wine, and oil increasing (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.7">Ps. iv. 7</reference>), and, if you <hi type="italic">destroy their vines and their fig-trees, you make all their mirth to cease,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.11-Hos.2.12">Hosea ii. 11, 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">They shall not</hi> now <hi type="italic">drink wine with a song</hi> and with huzzas, as they used to, but rather drink it with a sigh; nay, <hi type="italic">Strong drink shall be bitter to those that drink it,</hi> because they cannot but mingle their tears with it; or, through sickness, they have lost the relish of it. God has many ways to embitter wine and strong drink to those that love them and have the highest gust of them: distemper of body, anguish of mind, the ruin of the estate or country, will make the strong drink bitter and all the delights of sense tasteless and insipid. (2.) Music: <hi type="italic">The mirth of tabrets ceases, and the joy of the harp,</hi> which used to be at their feasts, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">ch. v. 12</reference>. The captives in Babylon hang their harps on the willow trees. In short, <hi type="italic">All joy is darkened;</hi> there is not a pleasant look to be seen, nor has any one power to force a smile; all <hi type="italic">the mirth of the land is gone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.11">v. 11</reference>); and, if it was that mirth which Solomon calls <hi type="italic">madness,</hi> there is no great loss of it. <div eID="gen15978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15979" type="x-p"/> VI. The cities will in a particular manner feel from these desolations of the country (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The city of confusion is broken, is broken down</hi> (so we read it); it lies exposed to invading powers, not only by the breaking down of its walls, but by the confusion that the inhabitants are in. <hi type="italic">Every house is shut up,</hi> perhaps by reason of the plague, which has burned or consumed the inhabitants, so that there are <hi type="italic">few men left,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.24.6">v. 6</reference>. Houses infected are usually shut up that no man may come in. Or they are shut up because they are deserted and uninhabited. <hi type="italic">There is a crying for wine,</hi> that is, for the spoiling of the vintage, so that there is likely to be no wine. <hi type="italic">In the city,</hi> in Jerusalem itself, that had been so much frequented, there shall be left nothing but <hi type="italic">desolation;</hi> grass shall grow in the streets, and <hi type="italic">the gate is smitten with destruction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.12">v. 12</reference>); all that used to pass and repass through the gate are smitten, and all the strength of the city is cut off. How soon can God make a city of order a city of confusion, and then it will soon be a city of desolation!
entries.2ed4c48badb429d003265566c5097ff1d39a2fee: <div eID="gen15979" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Hope in the End. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 718.)</title> <div sID="gen15980" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> When thus it shall be in the midst of the land among the people, <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> as the shaking of an olive tree, <hi type="italic">and</hi> as the gleaning grapes when the vintage is done. <hi type="super">14</hi> They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , they shall cry aloud from the sea. <hi type="super">15</hi> Wherefore glorify ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the fires, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel in the isles of the sea. <div eID="gen15980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15981" type="x-p"/> Here is mercy remembered in the midst of wrath. In Judah and Jerusalem, and the neighbouring countries, when they are overrun by the enemy, Sennacherib or Nebuchadnezzar, there shall be a remnant preserved from the general ruin, and it shall be a devout and pious remnant. And this method God usually observes when his judgments are abroad; he does not make a full end, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">ch. vi. 13</reference>. Or we may take it thus: Though the greatest part of mankind have all their comfort ruined by the emptying of the earth, and the making of that desolate, yet there are some few who understand their interests better, who have laid up their treasure in heaven and not in things below, and therefore can keep up their comfort and joy in God even <hi type="italic">when the earth mourns and fades away.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen15981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15982" type="x-p"/> I. The small number of this remnant, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.13">v. 13</reference>. When all goes to ruin <hi type="italic">there shall be as the shaking of an olive-tree, and the gleaning grapes,</hi> here and there one who shall escape the common calamity (as Noah and his family when the old world was drowned), that shall be able to sit down upon a heap of the ruins of all their creature comforts, and even then rejoice in the Lord (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.16-Hab.3.18">Hab. iii. 16-18</reference>), who, when all faces gather blackness, can lift up their heads with joy, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.26">Luke xxi. 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.28">28</reference>. These few are dispersed, and at a distance from each other, like the gleanings of the olive-tree; and they are concealed, hid under the leaves. The Lord only knows those that are his; the world does not. <div eID="gen15982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15983" type="x-p"/> II. The great devotion of this remnant, which is the greater for their having so narrowly escaped this great destruction (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall lift up their voice; they shall sing.</hi> 1. They shall sing for joy in their deliverance. When the mirth of carnal worldlings ceases the joy of the saints is as lively as ever; when the merry-hearted do sigh because the vine languishes the upright-hearted do sing because the covenant of grace, the fountain of their comforts and the foundation of their hopes, never fails. Those that rejoice in the Lord can rejoice in tribulation, and by faith may be in triumphs when all about them are in tears. 2. They shall sing to the glory and praise of God, shall sing not only for the mercy but <hi type="italic">for the majesty of the Lord.</hi> Their songs are awful and serious, and in their spiritual joys they have a reverend regard to the greatness of God, and keep at a humble distance when they attend him with their praises. The majesty of the Lord, which is matter of terror to wicked people, furnishes the saints with songs of praise. They shall sing for the magnificence, or transcendent excellency, of the Lord, shown both in his judgments and in his mercies; for we must sing, and sing unto him, of both, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.1">Ps. ci. 1</reference>. Those who have made, or are making, their escape from the land (that being emptied and made desolate) to the sea and the isles of the sea, shall thence cry aloud; their dispersion shall help to spread the knowledge of God, and they shall make even remote shores to ring with his praises. It is much for the honour of God if those who fear him rejoice in him, and praise him, even in the most melancholy times. <div eID="gen15983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15984" type="x-p"/> III. Their holy zeal to excite others to the same devotion (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.15">v. 15</reference>); they encourage their fellow-sufferers to do likewise. 1. Those who are <hi type="italic">in the fires,</hi> in the furnace of affliction, those fires by which the <hi type="italic">inhabitants of the earth are burned,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.24.6">v. 6</reference>. Or in the valleys, the low, dark, dirty places. 2. Those who are <hi type="italic">in the isles of the sea,</hi> whither they are banished, or are forced to flee for shelter, and hide themselves remote from all their friends. They went <hi type="italic">through fire and water</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Ps. lxvi. 12</reference>); yet in both let them glorify the Lord, and glory him as the Lord God of Israel. Those who through grace can glory in tribulation ought to glorify God in tribulation, and give him thanks for their comforts, which abound as their afflictions do abound. We must in every fire, even the hottest, in every isle, even the remotest, keep up our good thoughts of God. When, though he slay us, yet we trust in him—when, though for his sake we are killed all the day long, yet none of these things move us—then we glorify the Lord in the fires. Thus the three children, and the martyrs that sang at the stake.
entries.df4b2d9756a0db64ab345dba68d3880f10206fac: <div eID="gen15984" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouraging Prospects; Degeneracy Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 718.)</title> <div sID="gen15985" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, <hi type="italic">even</hi> glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously. <hi type="super">17</hi> Fear, and the pit, and the snare, <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon thee, O inhabitant of the earth. <hi type="super">18</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> he who fleeth from the noise of the fear shall fall into the pit; and he that cometh up out of the midst of the pit shall be taken in the snare: for the windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake. <hi type="super">19</hi> The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly. <hi type="super">20</hi> The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again. <hi type="super">21</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall punish the host of the high ones <hi type="italic">that are</hi> on high, and the kings of the earth upon the earth. <hi type="super">22</hi> And they shall be gathered together, <hi type="italic">as</hi> prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison, and after many days shall they be visited. <hi type="super">23</hi> Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously. <div eID="gen15985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15986" type="x-p"/> These verses, as those before, plainly speak, <div eID="gen15986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15987" type="x-p"/> I. Comfort to saints. They may be driven, by the common calamities of the places where they live, into <hi type="italic">the uttermost parts of the earth,</hi> or perhaps they are forced thither for their religion; but there they are singing, not sighing. Thence have we heard songs, and it is a comfort to us to hear them, to hear that good people carry their religion along with them even to the most distant regions, to hear that God visits them there and gives encouragement to hope that he will gather them thence, <reference osisRef="Deut.30.4">Deut. xxx. 4</reference>. And this is their song, <hi type="italic">even glory to the righteous:</hi> the word is singular, and may refer to <hi type="italic">the righteous God,</hi> who is just in all he has brought upon us. This is glorifying the Lord in the fires. Or the meaning may be, "These songs redound to the glory or beauty of the righteous that sing them." We do the greatest honour imaginable to ourselves when we employ ourselves in honouring and glorifying God. This may have reference to the sending of the gospel to the uttermost parts of the earth, as far as this island of ours, in the days of the Messiah, the glad tidings of which are echoed back in songs heard thence, from churches planted there, even glory to the righteous God, agreeing with the angels' song, <hi type="italic">Glory be to God in the highest,</hi> and glory to all righteous men; for the work of redemption was ordained before the world for our glory. <div eID="gen15987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15988" type="x-p"/> II. Terror to sinners. The prophet, having comforted himself and others with the prospect of a saved remnant, returns to lament the miseries he saw breaking in like a mighty torrent upon the earth: "<hi type="italic">But I said, My leanness! my leanness! woe unto me!</hi> The very thought of it frets me, and makes me lean," <reference osisRef="Isa.24.16">v. 16</reference>. He foresees, <div eID="gen15988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15989" type="x-p"/> 1. The prevalency of sin, that iniquity should abound (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously;</hi> this is itself a judgment, and that which provokes God to bring other judgments. (1.) Men are false to one another; there is no faith in man, but a universal dishonesty. Truth, that sacred bond of society, has departed, and there is nothing but treachery in men's dealings. See <reference osisRef="Jer.9.1-Jer.9.2">Jer. ix. 1, 2</reference>. (2.) They are all false to their God; as to him, and their covenant with him, the children of men are all treacherous dealers, and have dealt very treacherously with their God, in departing from their allegiance to him. This is the original, and this the aggravation, of the sin of the world; and, when men have been false to their God, how should they be true to any other? <div eID="gen15989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15990" type="x-p"/> 2. The prevalency of wrath and judgment for that sin. (2.) The inhabitants of the earth will be pursued from time to time, from place to place, by one mischief or other (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.17-Isa.24.18">v. 17, 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Fear, and the pit, and the snare</hi> (fear of the pit and the snare) are upon them wherever they are; for the sons of men know not what evil they may suddenly be snared in, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">Eccl. ix. 12</reference>. These three words seem to be chosen for the sake of an elegant paranomasia, or, as we now scornfully call it, a jungle of words: <hi type="italic">Pachad,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pachath,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pach;</hi> but the meaning is plain (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.18">v. 18</reference>), that <hi type="italic">evil pursues sinners</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.21">Prov. xiii. 21</reference>), that the curse shall overtake the disobedient (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.15">Deut. xxviii. 15</reference>), that those who are secure because they have escaped one judgment know not how soon another may arrest them. What this prophet threatens all the inhabitants of the earth with another makes part of the judgment of Moab, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.43">Jer. xlviii. 43, 44</reference>. But it is a common instance of the calamitous state of human life that when we seek to avoid one mischief we fall into a worse, and that the end of one trouble is often the beginning of another; so that we are least safe when we are most secure. (2.) The earth itself will be shaken to pieces. It will be literally so at last, when all <hi type="italic">the works therein shall be burnt up;</hi> and it is often figuratively so before that period. <hi type="italic">The windows from on high are open</hi> to pour down wrath, as in the universal deluge. <hi type="italic">Upon the wicked God shall rain snares</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Ps. xi. 6</reference>); and, the fountains of the great deep being broken up, <hi type="italic">the foundations of the earth do shake</hi> of course, the frame of nature is unhinged, and all is in confusion. See how elegantly this is expressed (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.19-Isa.24.20">v. 19, 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">The earth is utterly broken down; it is clean dissolved; it is moved exceedingly,</hi> moved out of its place. <hi type="italic">God shakes heaven and earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag. ii. 6</reference>. See the misery of those who lay up their treasure in the things of the earth and mind those things; they place their confidence in that which will shortly be <hi type="italic">utterly broken down and dissolved. The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard;</hi> so unsteady, so uncertain, are all the motions of these things. Worldly men dwell in it as in a palace, as in a castle, as in an impregnable tower; but <hi type="italic">it shall be removed like a cottage,</hi> so easily, so suddenly, and with so little loss to the great landlord. The pulling down of the earth will be but like the pulling down of <hi type="italic">a cottage,</hi> which the country is willing to be rid of, because it does but harbour beggars; and therefore no care is taken to rebuild it: It <hi type="italic">shall fall, and not rise again;</hi> but there shall be new heavens and a new earth, in which shall dwell nothing but righteousness. But what is it that shakes the earth thus and sinks it? It is the transgression thereof that shall be heavy upon it. Note, Sin is a burden to the whole creation; it is a heavy burden, a burden under which it groans now and will sink at last. Sin is the ruin of states, and kingdoms, and families; they fall under the weight of that <hi type="italic">talent of lead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.5.7-Zech.5.8">Zech. v. 7, 8</reference>. (3.) God will have a particular controversy with the kings and great men of the earth (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">He will punish the host of the high ones.</hi> Hosts of princes are no more before God than hosts of common men; what can a host of high ones do with their combined force when the Most High, the Lord of hosts, contends with them to abase their height, and scatter their hosts, and break all their confederacies? The high ones, that are on high, that are puffed up with their height and grandeur, that think themselves so high that they are out of the reach of any danger, God will visit upon them all their pride and cruelty, with which they have oppressed and injured their neighbours and subjects, and it shall now return upon their own heads. <hi type="italic">The kings of the earth</hi> shall now be reckoned with <hi type="italic">upon the earth,</hi> to show that verily there is a God that judges in the earth and will render to the proudest of kings according to the fruit of their doings. Let those that are trampled upon by the high ones of the earth comfort themselves with this, that though they cannot, dare not, must not, resist them, yet there is a God that will call them to an account, that will triumph over them upon their own dunghill: for the earth they are kings of is in the eye of God no better. This is general only. It is particularly foretold (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.22">v. 22</reference>) that they shall be <hi type="italic">gathered together as prisoners,</hi> convicted condemned prisoners, are <hi type="italic">gathered in the pit,</hi> or dungeon, and there they shall <hi type="italic">be shut up</hi> under close confinement. The kings and high ones, who took all possible liberty themselves, and took a pride and pleasure in shutting up others, shall now be themselves shut up. Let not the free man glory in his freedom, any more than the strong man in his strength, for he knows not what restraints he is reserved for. But <hi type="italic">after many days they shall be visited,</hi> either, [1.] They shall be visited in wrath; it is the same word, in another form, that is used (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.21">v. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">the Lord shall punish</hi> them; they shall be reserved to the day of execution, as condemned prisoners are, and as fallen angels are <hi type="italic">reserved in chains of darkness to the judgment of the great day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.6">Jude 6</reference>. Let this account for the delays of divine vengeance; sentence is not executed speedily, because execution-day has not yet come, and perhaps will not come till after many days; but it is certain that the wicked is reserved for the day of destruction, and is therefore preserved in the mean time, but <hi type="italic">shall be brought forth to the day of wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job xxi. 30</reference>. Let us therefore judge nothing before the time. [2.] They shall be visited in mercy, and be discharged from their imprisonment, and shall again obtain, if not their dignity, yet their liberty. Nebuchadnezzar, in his conquests, made many kings and princes his captives, and kept them in the dungeon in Babylon, and, among the rest, Jehoiachin King of Judah; but after many days, when Nebuchadnezzar's head was laid, his son visited them, and granted (as should seem) some reviving to them all in their bondage; for it is made an instance of his particular kindness to Jehoiachin that he <hi type="italic">set his throne above the throne of the rest of the kings that were with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.52.32">Jer. lii. 32</reference>. If we apply this to the general state of mankind, it imports a revolution of conditions; those that were high are punished, those that were punished are relieved, after many days, that none in this world may be secure though their condition be ever so prosperous, nor any despair though their condition be ever so deplorable. <div eID="gen15990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15991" type="x-p"/> 3. Glory to God in all this, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">v. 23</reference>. When all this comes to pass, when the proud enemies of God's church are humbled and brought down, (1.) Then it shall appear, beyond contradiction, that the Lord reigns, which is always true, but not always alike evident. When the kings of the earth are punished for their tyranny and oppression, then it is proclaimed and proved to all the world that God is King of kings—King above them, by whom they are accountable—that he reigns as <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> of all hosts, of their hosts,—that he reigns <hi type="italic">in Mount Zion, and in Jerusalem,</hi> in his church, for the honour and welfare of that, pursuant to the promises on which that is founded, reigns in his word and ordinances,—that he reigns <hi type="italic">before his ancients,</hi> before all his saints, especially before his ministers, the elders of his church, who have their eye upon all the out-goings of his power and providence, and, in all these events, observe his hand. God's ancients, the old disciples, the experienced Christians, that have often, when they have been perplexed, gone into the sanctuary of God in Zion and Jerusalem, and acquainted themselves with his manifestations of himself there, shall see more than others of God's dominion and sovereignty in these operations of his providence. (2.) Then it shall appear, beyond comparison, that he reigns <hi type="italic">gloriously,</hi> in such brightness and lustre that <hi type="italic">the moon shall be confounded and the sun ashamed,</hi> as the smaller lights are eclipsed and extinguished by the greater. Great men, who thought themselves to have as bright a lustre and as vast a dominion as the sun and moon, shall be ashamed when God appears above them, much more when he appears against them. Then shall <hi type="italic">their faces be filled with shame,</hi> that they may seek God's name. The eastern nations worshipped the sun and moon; but, when God shall appear so gloriously for his people against his and their enemies, all these pretended deities shall be ashamed that ever they received the homage of their deluded worshippers. The glory of the Creator infinitely outshines the glory of the brightest creatures. In the great day, when the Judge of heaven and earth shall shine forth in his glory, <hi type="italic">the sun shall</hi> by his transcendent lustre <hi type="italic">be turned into darkness and the moon into blood.</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.24"/> <div eID="gen15991" type="x-p"/>

entries.7d534d7b49df7f1dce166ebc66ef42a1f5d7f873: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8735"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 24</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.24.1-Isa.24.23">Is 24:1-23</reference>. The Last Times of the World in General, and of Judah and the Church in Particular.</title> <div sID="gen14482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The four chapters (the twenty-fourth through the twenty-seventh) form one continuous poetical prophecy: descriptive of the dispersion and successive calamities of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.1-Isa.24.12">Is 24:1-12</reference>); the preaching of the Gospel by the first Hebrew converts throughout the world (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.13-Isa.24.16">Is 24:13-16</reference>); the judgments on the adversaries of the Church and its final triumph (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.16-Isa.24.23">Is 24:16-23</reference>); thanksgiving for the overthrow of the apostate faction (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.1-Isa.25.12">Is 25:1-12</reference>), and establishment of the righteous in lasting peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.1-Isa.26.21">Is 26:1-21</reference>); judgment on leviathan and entire purgation of the Church (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.1-Isa.27.13">Is 27:1-13</reference>). Having treated of the several nations in particular--</hi>Babylon, Philistia, Moab, Syria, Israel, Egypt, Edom, and Tyre (the miniature representative of all, as all kingdoms flocked into it)--he passes to the last times of the world at large and of Judah the representative and future head of the churches.<div eID="gen14482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14483" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8735"/><hi type="bold">1. the earth--</hi>rather, "the land" of Judah (so in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.3">Is 24:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.6">5, 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.1.2">Joe 1:2</reference>). The desolation under Nebuchadnezzar prefigured that under Titus. <div eID="gen14483" type="x-p"/>
entries.a71aeb18477e8d2f262e4f1afdaf62343962ee95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8736"/><div sID="gen14484" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8736"/><hi type="bold">2. as with the people, so with the priest--</hi>All alike shall share the same calamity: no favored class shall escape (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.12">Eze 7:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.9">Ho 4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Re 6:15</reference>). <div eID="gen14484" type="x-p"/>
entries.e49ba5afb77dc15a1b50fe279c0ac4c7cff517e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8737"/><div sID="gen14485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8737"/><hi type="bold">4. world--</hi>the kingdom of Israel; as in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Is 13:11</reference>, Babylon.<div eID="gen14485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">haughty--</hi>literally, "the height" of the people: abstract for concrete, that is, the high people; even the nobles share the general distress. <div eID="gen14486" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c07ac45c890274abb487f73f7d51962856bb5ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8738"/><div sID="gen14487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8738"/><hi type="bold">5. earth--</hi>rather, "the land."<div eID="gen14487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defiled under ... inhabitants--</hi>namely, with innocent blood (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.11">Ge 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.35.33">Nu 35:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.38">Psa 106:38</reference>).<div eID="gen14488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laws ... ordinance ... everlasting covenant--</hi>The moral laws, positive statutes, and national covenant designed to be for ever between God and them. <div eID="gen14489" type="x-p"/>
entries.070032ba7bacc8a7175c016087087bb03eacb4f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8739"/><div sID="gen14490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8739"/><hi type="bold">6. earth--</hi>the land.<div eID="gen14490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burned--</hi>namely, with the consuming wrath of heaven: either internally, as in <reference osisRef="Job.30.30">Job 30:30</reference> [Rosenmuller]; or externally, the prophet has before his eyes the people being consumed with the withering dryness of their doomed land (so <reference osisRef="Joel.1.10">Joe 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>), [Maurer]. <div eID="gen14491" type="x-p"/>

entries.29a78f859c6e104dc98bf34b98c453e45a30a58f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8742"/><div sID="gen14495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8742"/><hi type="bold">9. with a song--</hi>the usual accompaniment of feasts.<div eID="gen14495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strong drink--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Is 5:11</reference>). "Date wine" [Horsley].<div eID="gen14496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bitter--</hi>in consequence of the national calamities. <div eID="gen14497" type="x-p"/>
entries.5cad4f1e8881f40dbb8501a33d9a4889c426e3b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8743"/><div sID="gen14498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8743"/><hi type="bold">10. city of confusion--</hi>rather, "desolation." Horsley translates, "The city is broken down; it is a ruin."<div eID="gen14498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shut up--</hi>through fear; or rather, "choked up by ruins." <div eID="gen14499" type="x-p"/>
entries.b06dad99073c4996216d390336c6a709b6b5420e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8744"/><div sID="gen14500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8744"/><hi type="bold">11. crying for wine--</hi>to drown their sorrows in drink (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Is 16:9</reference>); <reference osisRef="Joel.1.5">Joe 1:5</reference>, written about the same time, resembles this. <div eID="gen14500" type="x-p"/>
entries.37b25f7a0a3202bcc524080b1f96f141aae59b7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8745"/><div sID="gen14501" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8745"/><hi type="bold">12. with destruction--</hi>rather "crash" [Gesenius]. "With a great tumult the gate is battered down" [Horsley]. <div eID="gen14501" type="x-p"/>
entries.2abd0db0b30d0692c68f7f184fb297657cd7a643: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8746"/><div sID="gen14502" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8746"/><hi type="bold">13. the land--</hi>Judea. Put the comma after "land," not after "people." "There shall be among the people (a remnant left), as the shaking (the after-picking) of an olive tree"; as in gathering olives, a few remain on the highest boughs (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.5">Is 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen14502" type="x-p"/>
entries.a486ca637c1fdce019615fc572ef336c2050b4ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8747"/><div sID="gen14503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8747"/><hi type="bold">14. They--</hi>those who are left: the remnant.<div eID="gen14503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sing for the majesty of the Lord--</hi>sing a thanksgiving for the goodness of the Lord, who has so mercifully preserved them.<div eID="gen14504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the sea--</hi>from the distant lands beyond the sea, whither they have escaped. <div eID="gen14505" type="x-p"/>
entries.118c4101a05f3b590d376037f940180ccb44b137: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8748"/><div sID="gen14506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8748"/><hi type="bold">15. in the fires--</hi>Vitringa translates, "in the caves." Could it mean the fires of affliction (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1Pe 1:7</reference>)? They were exiles at the time. The fires only loose the carnal bonds off the soul, without injuring a hair, as in the case of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego. Lowth reads, in the islands (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.18">Eze 26:18</reference>). Rather translate for "fires," "in the regions of morning light," that is, the east, in antithesis to the "isles of the sea," that is, the west [Maurer]. Wheresoever ye be scattered, east or west, still glorify the Lord (Mal 1:11). <div eID="gen14506" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac0216fd30f210279e162304baacd5393172dfa0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8749"/><div sID="gen14507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8749"/>16. Songs to God come in together to Palestine from distant lands, as a grand chorus.<div eID="gen14507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory to the righteous--</hi>the burden of the songs (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.2">Is 26:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.7">7</reference>). Amidst exile, the loss of their temple, and all that is dear to man, their confidence in God is unshaken. These songs recall the joy of other times and draw from Jerusalem in her present calamities, the cry, "My leanness." Horsley translates, "glory to the Just One"; then My leanness expresses his sense of man's corruption, which led the Jews, "the treacherous dealers" (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.11">Jr 5:11</reference>), to crucify the Just One; and his deficiency of righteousness which made him need to be clothed with the righteousness of the Just One (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.15">Psa 106:15</reference>).<div eID="gen14508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14509" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">treacherous dealers--</hi>the foreign nations that oppress Jerusalem, and overcome it by stratagem (so in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">Is 21:2</reference>) [Barnes]. <div eID="gen14509" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c0c2b1a1ed6069cfcf8417d0a8effd69da7cc8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8750"/><div sID="gen14510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8750"/>17. This verse explains the wretchedness spoken of in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.16">Is 24:16</reference>. Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.43">Jr 48:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.44">44</reference>) uses the same words. They are proverbial; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.18">Is 24:18</reference> expressing that the inhabitants were nowhere safe; if they escaped one danger, they fell into another, and worse, on the opposite side (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.19">Am 5:19</reference>). "Fear" is the term applied to the cords with feathers of all colors which, when fluttered in the air, scare beasts into the pitfall, or birds into the snare. Horsley makes the connection. Indignant at the treatment which the Just One received, the prophet threatens the guilty land with instant vengeance. <div eID="gen14510" type="x-p"/>
entries.2116cb6773bb9128f6129ea67b7ed6ccda987dbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8751"/><div sID="gen14511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8751"/><hi type="bold">18. noise of ... fear--</hi>the shout designed to rouse the game and drive it into the pitfall.<div eID="gen14511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">windows ... open--</hi>taken from the account of the deluge (<reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Ge 7:11</reference>); the flood-gates. So the final judgments of fire on the apostate world are compared to the deluge (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.5-2Pet.3.7">2Pe 3:5-7</reference>). <div eID="gen14512" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ac0db942cd68f1129031115e4cede95d0a49290: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8752"/><div sID="gen14513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8752"/><hi type="bold">19. earth--</hi>the land: image from an earthquake. <div eID="gen14513" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e9d1f458feece01e6a8cb14634b0203bec27e35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8753"/><div sID="gen14514" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8753"/><hi type="bold">20. removed like a cottage--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Is 1:8</reference>). Here, a hanging couch, suspended from the trees by cords, such as Niebuhr describes the Arab keepers of lands as having, to enable them to keep watch, and at the same time to be secure from wild beasts. Translate, "Shall wave to and fro like a hammock" swung about by the wind.<div eID="gen14514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavy upon it--</hi>like an overwhelming burden.<div eID="gen14515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14516" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not rise again--</hi>not meaning, that it never would rise (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Is 24:23</reference>), but in those convulsions it would not rise, it would surely fall. <div eID="gen14516" type="x-p"/>
entries.d71e253e98acf2dbbd4bf330efe679ee422e1b9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8754"/><div sID="gen14517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8754"/><hi type="bold">21. host of ... high ones--</hi>the heavenly host, that is, either the visible host of heaven (the present economy of nature, affected by the sun, moon, and stars, the objects of idolatry, being abolished, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Is 65:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">60:19</reference>, simultaneously with the corrupt polity of men); or rather, "the invisible rulers of the darkness of this world," as the antithesis to "kings of the earth" shows. Angels, moreover, preside, as it were, over kingdoms of the world (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Da 10:13</reference>, 20, 21). <div eID="gen14517" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f5b3f2e1789da1e236d730fd3d8aa33e9af0fb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8755"/><div sID="gen14518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8755"/><hi type="bold">22. in the pit--</hi>rather, "for the pit" [Horsley]. "In the dungeon" [Maurer]. Image from captives thrust together into a dungeon.<div eID="gen14518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prison--</hi>that is, as in a prison. This sheds light on the disputed passage, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.19">1Pe 3:19</reference>, where also the prison is figurative: The "shutting up" of the Jews in Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar, and again under Titus, was to be followed by a visitation of mercy "after many days"--seventy years in the case of the former--the time is not yet elapsed in the case of the latter. Horsley takes "visited" in a bad sense, namely, in wrath, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.14">Is 26:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Is 29:6</reference>; the punishment being the heavier in the fact of the delay. Probably a double visitation is intended, deliverance to the elect, wrath to hardened unbelievers; as <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Is 24:23</reference> plainly contemplates judgments on proud sinners, symbolized by the "sun" and "moon." <div eID="gen14519" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4fc9bc630eea3fcbe745325a1f8ee9b2279e6de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8756"/><div sID="gen14520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8756"/>23. (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>). Still future: of which Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem amidst hosannas was a pledge.<div eID="gen14520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his ancients--</hi>the elders of His people; or in general, His ancient people, the Jews. After the overthrow of the world kingdoms. Jehovah's shall be set up with a splendor exceeding the light of the sun and moon under the previous order of things (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">Is 60:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.20">20</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.24"/>

entries.c448c0b523ca098800b35ad9bbf6247438b0f6c9: <div eID="gen27460" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27461" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27462" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27462" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27461" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27463" type="x-p"/> Dreadful judgments impending over the people of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1-Isa.24.4">Isa 24:1-4</reference>. Particular enumeration of the horrid impieties which provoked the Divine vengeance, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.5">Isa 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.6">Isa 24:6</reference>. Great political wretchedness of the transgressors, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.7-Isa.24.12">Isa 24:7-12</reference>. The calamities shall be so great that only a small remnant shall be left in the land, as it were the gleanings of the vintage, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.13">Isa 24:13</reference>. The rest, scattered over the different countries, spread there the knowledge of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.14-Isa.24.16">Isa 24:14-16</reference>. Strong figures by which the great distress and long captivity of the transgressors are set forth, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.17-Isa.24.22">Isa 24:17-22</reference>. Gracious promise of a redemption from captivity; and of an extension of the kingdom of God in the latter days, attended with such glorious circumstances as totally to eclipse the light and splendor of the previous dispensation, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa 24:23</reference>. <div eID="gen27463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27464" type="x-p"/> From the thirteenth chapter to the twenty-third inclusive, the fate of several cities and nations is denounced: of Babylon, of the Philistines, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre. After having foretold the destruction of the foreign nations, enemies of Judah, the prophet declares the judgments impending on the people of God themselves for their wickedness and apostasy, and the desolation that shall be brought on their whole country. <div eID="gen27464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27465" type="x-p"/> The twenty-fourth and the three following chapters seem to have been delivered about the same time: before the destruction of Moab by Shalmaneser; see <reference osisRef="Isa.25.10">Isa 25:10</reference>, consequently, before the destruction of Samaria; probably in the beginning of Hezekiah's reign. But concerning the particular subject of the twenty-fourth chapter interpreters are not at all agreed: some refer it to the desolation caused by the invasion of Shalmaneser; others to the invasion of Nebuchadnezzar; and others to the destruction of the city and nation by the Romans. Vitringa is singular in his opinion, who applies it to the persecution of Antiochus Epiphanes. Perhaps it may have a view to all of the three great desolations of the country, by Shalmaneser, by Nebuchadnezzar, and by the Romans; especially the last, to which some parts of it may seem more peculiarly applicable. However, the prophet chiefly employs general images; such as set forth the greatness and universality of the ruin and desolation that is to be brought upon the country by these great revolutions, involving all orders and degrees of men, changing entirely the face of things, and destroying the whole polity, both religious and civil; without entering into minute circumstances, or necessarily restraining it by particular marks to one great event, exclusive of others of the same kind. - L.
entries.8d6035158c6364d5028ec5faf77810500cba3fa6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27466" type="x-p"/> The world languisheth - The world is the same with the land; that is, the kingdoms of Judah and Israel, orbis Israeliticus. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Isa 13:11</reference> (note).
entries.b43f65b53f20eafa5b81c4d7cce5a3b40d92d96f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27467" type="x-p"/> The laws "The law" - תורה torah, singular: so read the Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee.
entries.47ed5a77052a1fe7b17a4e852ca3f9a7fccce6da: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27468" type="x-p"/> Are burned "Are destroyed" - For חרו charu, read חרבו charebu. See the Septuagint, Syriac, Chaldee and Symmachus.
entries.5989144117f5dbb8435dfe5a04c3fb6fd0a1aba6: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27469" type="x-p"/> The mirth, etc. - שאון sheon, the noise. גאון geon, the pride, is the reading of three of De Rossi's MSS., with the Septuagint and Arabic.
entries.37748ab9d5b9f41fe77c18e58b2558494817d1c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27470" type="x-p"/> Strong drink "Palm wine" - This is the proper meaning of the word שכר shechar, σικερα. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Isa 5:11</reference>. All enjoyment shall cease: the sweetest wine shall become bitter to their taste.
entries.628f1abe28ca261d9d67c2dd135d73aae3be7997: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27471" type="x-p"/> All joy is darkened "All gladness is passed away" - For ערבה arebah, darkened, read עברה aberah, passed away, transposing a letter. Houbigant, Secker. Five of Dr. Kennicott's and five of De Rossi's MSS., several ancients add כל col, all, after משוש mesos: the Septuagint adds the same word before it.
entries.0c18abc8afbb05fc068acfdcfc1389c6dd5ec898: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen27471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27472" type="x-p"/> They shall lift up their voice "But these shall lift up their voice" - That is, they that escaped out of these calamities. The great distresses brought upon Israel and Judah drove the people away, and dispersed them all over the neighboring countries: they fled to Egypt, to Asia Minor, to the islands and the coasts of Greece. They were to be found in great numbers in most of the principal cities of these countries. Alexandria was in a great measure peopled by them. They had synagogues for their worship in many places, and were greatly instrumental in propagating the knowledge of the true God among these heathen nations, and preparing them for the reception of Christianity. This it what the prophet seems to mean by the celebration of the name of Jehovah in the waters, in the distant coasts, and in the uttermost parts of the land. מים mayim, the waters; ὑδωρ, Sept.; ὑδατα, Theod.; not מים miyam from the sea.
entries.1cdbc2a93f9af3d52ad2c3d10866344cf173bc0c: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen27472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27473" type="x-p"/> In the isles of the sea "In the distant coasts of the sea" - For בארים beurim, in the valleys, I suppose we ought to read באיים beiyim, in the isles, which is in a great degree justified by the repetition of the word in the next member of the sentence, with the addition of הים haiyam, the sea, to vary the phrase, exactly in the manner of the prophet. איים iyim is a word chiefly applied to any distant countries, especially those lying on the Mediterranean Sea. Others conjecture ביארים biorim, בהרים beharim, באמים beummim, בעמים beammim, בחורים bechorim, באורים beurim, a באר bar, illustrate - Le Clerc. Twenty-three MSS. of Kennicott's, many of De Rossi's, and some of my own, read באורים beorim, in the valleys. The Septuagint do not acknowledge the reading of the text, expressing here only the word איים iyim, εν ταις νησοις, in the islands, and that not repeated. But MSS. Pachom. and 1. D. 2 supply in this place the defect in the other copies of the Septuagint thus, Δια τουτο ἡ δοξα Κυριου εσται εν ταις νησοις της θαλασσης· εν ταις νησοις το ονομα του Κυριου Θεου Ισραηλ ενδοξον εσται· "Therefore the glory of the Lord shall be in the isles of the sea: in the islands shall the name of the Lord God of Israel be glorified." <div eID="gen27473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27474" type="x-p"/> Kimchi says, that by באורים beurim, in the valleys is meant the cities, because they were generally built in valleys. The Vulgate has in doctrinis, and so my old MS., in techingis. Coverdale translates, Praise the name of the Lord God of Israel in the valleys and in the floodis. It should not be revered in the fires; none of the ancient Versions understood it thus. According to which the Septuagint had in their Hebrew copy באיים beiyim, repeated afterwards, not בארים beurim.
entries.301b7d12fdc47613e715a0a42802dc03ca01c197: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen27474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27475" type="x-p"/> But I said - The prophet speaks in the person of the inhabitants of the land still remaining there, who should be pursued by Divine vengeance, and suffer repeated distresses from the inroads and depredations of their powerful enemies. Agreeably to what he said before in a general denunciation of these calamities: - "Though there be a tenth part remaining in it; <div eID="gen27475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27476" type="x-p"/> Even this shall undergo a repeated destruction." <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Isa 6:13</reference> (note). See the note there. - L. <div eID="gen27476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27477" type="x-p"/> My leanness, my leanness - Or, my secret; so the Vulgate, Montanus, and my old MS; רזן razan has this meaning in Chaldee; but in Hebrew it signifies to make lean, to waste. This sentence in the Hebrew has a strange connection of uncouth sounds: ואמר רזי לי רזי לי אוי לי בוגדים בגדו ובגד בגדים בגרו Vaomer, razi li razi li, oi li, bogedim bagadu, ubeged bogedim bagadu. This may be equalled by the translation in my Old MS. Bible: And I seide, my priveye thinge to me: my priveye thinge to me: woo to me: The lawe breykynge thei breken: and in lawe brekynge of the overdon thingis, they breken the lawe. <div eID="gen27477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27478" type="x-p"/> The treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously "The plunderers plunder" - See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">Isa 21:2</reference>.
entries.c1c2fd4a436e486ea39ff93e7af450e4ba7eb749: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen27478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27479" type="x-p"/> Fear, and the pit "The terror, the pit" - If they escape one calamity, another shall overtake them. "As if a man should flee from a lion, and a bear should overtake him: <div eID="gen27479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27480" type="x-p"/> Or should betake himself to his house, and lean his hand on the wall, <div eID="gen27480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27481" type="x-p"/> And a serpent should bite him." <reference osisRef="Amo.5.19">Amo 5:19</reference>. "For," as our Savior expressed it in a like parabolical manner, "wheresoever the carcass is there shall the eagles be gathered together," <reference osisRef="Mat.24.28">Mat 24:28</reference>. The images are taken from the different methods of hunting and taking wild beasts, which were anciently in use. The terror was a line strung with feathers of all colors which fluttering in the air scared and frightened the beasts into the toils, or into the pit which was prepared for them. Nec est mirum, cum maximos ferarum greges linea pennis distincta contineat, et in insidias agat, ab ipso effectu dicta formido. Seneca de Ira, 2:12. The pit or pitfall, fovea; digged deep in the ground, and covered over with green boughs, turf, etc., in order to deceive them, that they might fall into it unawares. The snare, or toils, indago; a series of nets, inclosing at first a great space of ground, in which the wild beasts were known to be; and then drawn in by degrees into a narrower compass, till they were at last closely shut up, and entangled in them. - L. <div eID="gen27481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27482" type="x-p"/> For מכול mikkol, a MS. reads מפני mippeney, as it is in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.44">Jer 48:44</reference>, and so the Vulgate and Chaldee. But perhaps it is only, like the latter, a Hebraism, and means no more than the simple preposition מ mem. See <reference osisRef="Psa.102.6">Psa 102:6</reference>. For it does not appear that the terror was intended to scare the wild beasts by its noise. The paronomasia is very remarkable; פחד pachad, פחת pachath, פך pach: and that it was a common proverbial form, appears from Jeremiah's repeating it in the same words, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.43">Jer 48:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.44">Jer 48:44</reference>.
entries.25dd0895e3752ff176cbd3772a5c13791c17cc3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen27482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27483" type="x-p"/> Out of the midst of the pit "From the pit" - For מתוך mittoch, from the midst of, a MS. reads מן min, from, as it is in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.44">Jer 48:44</reference>; and so likewise the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate.
entries.297d2e330a72bcb5277b10312e99630980c09ede: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen27483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27484" type="x-p"/> The earth "The land" - הארץ haarets, forte delendum ה he, ut ex praecedente ortum. Vid. seqq. - Secker. "Probably the ה he, in הארץ haarets, should be blotted out, as having arisen from the preceding."
entries.6fc841a822967b7a040f0b012d5000d68693c368: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen27484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27485" type="x-p"/> Like a cottage "Like a lodge for a night" - See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Isa 1:8</reference>.
entries.5ff1589838620d974fe606cb749982682ccf5429: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen27485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27486" type="x-p"/> On high - upon the earth - That is, the ecclesiastical and civil polity of the Jews, which shall be destroyed. The nation shall continue in a state of depression and dereliction for a long time. The image seems to be taken from the practice of the great monarchs of that time; who, when they had thrown their wretched captives into a dungeon, never gave themselves the trouble of inquiring about them; but let them lie a long time in that miserable condition, wholly destitute of relief, and disregarded. God shall at length revisit and restore his people in the last age: and then the kingdom of God shall be established in such perfection, as wholly to obscure and eclipse the glory of the temporary, typical, preparative kingdom now subsisting.
entries.e1efcdbefd68f75c41a80573d8a37bf6fa302fc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen27486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27487" type="x-p"/> Before his ancients gloriously - In the sigt of their olde men he schal ben glorified. Old MS. Bible. "The figurative language of the prophets is taken from the analogy between the world natural and an empire or kingdom considered as a world politic. Accordingly the whole world natural, consisting of heaven and earth, signifies the whole world politic, consisting of thrones and people; or so much of it as is considered in prophecy: and the things in that world signify the analogous things in this. For the heavens and the things thereto signify thrones and dignities, and those who enjoy them; and the earth with the things thereon, the inferior people; and the lowest parts of the earth, called hades or hell, the lowest or most miserable part of them. Great earthquakes, and the shaking of heaven and earth, are put for the shaking of kingdoms, so as to distract and overthrow them; the creating a new heaven and earth, and the passing away of an old one, or the beginning and end of a world, for the rise and ruin of a body politic signified thereby. The sun, for the whole species and race of kings, in the kingdoms of the world politic; the moon, for the body of the common people, considered as the king's wife; the stars, for subordinate princes and great men; or for bishops and rulers of the people of God, when the sun is Christ: setting of the sun, moon, and stars. darkening the sun, Turning the moon into blood and falling of the stars, for the ceasing of a kingdom." Sir 1. Newton's Observations on the Prophecies, Part I., chap. 2. <div eID="gen27487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27488" type="x-p"/> These observations are of great consequence and use, in explaining the phraseology of the prophets.  <chapter eID="Isa.24"/> <div eID="gen27488" type="x-p"/>

entries.a081d9afe1002bc2a196623bc201929bcb644fa1: <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1-Isa.24.3">Isa 24:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen13123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13124" type="x-p"/> It is thoroughly characteristic of Isaiah, that the commencement of this prophecy, like <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">Isa 19:1</reference>, places us at once in the very midst of the catastrophe, and condenses the contents of the subsequent picture of judgment into a few rapid, vigorous, vivid, and comprehensive clauses (like <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Isa 15:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1">Isa 23:1</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa 33:1</reference>). <hi type="italic">“Behold, Jehovah emptieth the earth, and layeth it waste, and marreth its form, and scattereth its inhabitants. And it happeneth, as to the people, so to the priest; as to the servant, so to his master; as to the maid, so to her mistress; as to the buyer, so to the seller; as to the lender, so to the borrower; as to the creditor, so to the debtor. Emptying the earth is emptied, and plundering is plundered: for Jehovah hat spoken this word.”</hi> The question, whether the prophet is speaking of a past of future judgment, which is one of importance to the interpretation of the whole, is answered by the fact that with Isaiah “<hi type="italic">hinnēh</hi>” (behold) always refers to something future (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Isa 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">Isa 19:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27">Isa 30:27</reference>, etc.). And it is only in his case, that we do meet with prophecies commencing so immediately with <hi type="italic">hinnēh</hi>. Those in Jeremiah which approach this the most nearly (viz., <reference osisRef="Jer.47.2">Jer 47:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.35">Jer 49:35</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.51.1">Isa 51:1</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>) do indeed commence with <hi type="italic">hinnēh</hi>, but not without being preceded by an introductory formula. The opening “behold” corresponds to the confirmatory “for Jehovah hath spoken,” which is always employed by Isaiah at the close of statements with regard to the future and occurs chiefly,<note placement="foot">Vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.1.20">Isa 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.17">Isa 21:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.25">Isa 22:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.8">Isa 25:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.5">Isa 40:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">Isa 58:14</reference>; also compare <reference osisRef="Isa.19.4">Isa 19:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.13">Isa 16:13</reference>, and Isa 37:22.</note> though not exclusively,<note placement="foot">Vid., Oba 1:18, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.8">Joe 3:8</reference>, Mic 4:4; 1Ki 14:11.</note> in the book of Isaiah, whom we may recognise in the detailed description in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.2">Isa 24:2</reference> (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.2.12-Isa.2.16">Isa 2:12-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.2-Isa.3.3">Isa 3:2-3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.18-Isa.3.23">Isa 3:18-23</reference>, as compared with <reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Isa 9:13</reference>; also with the description of judgment in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.2-Isa.19.4">Isa 19:2-4</reference>, which closes in a similar manner). Thus at the very outset we meet with Isaiah’s peculiarities; and Caspari is right in saying that no prophecy could possibly commence with more of the characteristics of Isaiah than the prophecy before us. The play upon words commences at the very outset. <hi type="italic">Bâkak</hi> and <hi type="italic">bâlak</hi> (compare the Arabic <hi type="italic">ballūka</hi>, a blank, naked desert) have the same ring, just as in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.11">Nah 2:11</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.24.3">Isa 24:3</reference>, and Jer 51:2. The <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> futures are intentionally written like verbs <hi type="italic">Pe</hi>-<hi type="italic">Vâv</hi> (<hi type="italic">tibbōk</hi> and <hi type="italic">tibbōz</hi>, instead of <hi type="italic">tibbak</hi> and <hi type="italic">tibbaz</hi>), for the purpose of making them rhyme with the infinitive absolutes (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.22.13">Isa 22:13</reference>). So, again, <hi type="italic">caggebirtâh</hi> is so written instead of <hi type="italic">cigbirtâh</hi>, to produce a greater resemblance to the opening syllable of the other words.
