The form נשׁה is interchanged with נשׁא) (as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.2">1Sa 22:2</reference>), or, according to Kimchi’s way of writing it, with נשׁא) (written with <hi type="italic">tzere</hi>), just as in other passages we meet with נשׁא along with נשׁה, and, judging from Arab. <hi type="italic">ns'</hi>, to postpone or credit, the former is the primary form. <hi type="italic">Nōsheh</hi> is the creditor, and בו נשׁא אשׁר is not the person who has borrowed of him, but, as נשה invariably signifies to credit (<hi type="italic">hiphil</hi>, to give credit), the person whom he credits (with ב <hi type="italic">obj.</hi>, like בּ נגשׂ in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Isa 9:3</reference>), not “the person through whom he is נשׁא)” (Hitzig on <reference osisRef="Jer.15.10">Jer 15:10</reference>). Hence, “lender and borrower, creditor and debtor” (or taker of credit). It is a judgment which embraces all, without distinction of rank and condition; and it is a universal one, not merely throughout the whole of the <hi type="italic">land</hi> of Israel (as even Drechsler renders הארץ), but in all the earth; for as Arndt correctly observes, הארץ signifies “the earth” in this passage, including, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa 11:4</reference>, the ethical New Testament idea of “the world” (<hi type="italic">kosmos</hi>).
entries.039d850ed2e9634312f88563c1ac593cb78c9039: <reference osisRef="Isa.24.4-Isa.24.9">Isa 24:4-9</reference> <div eID="gen13124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13125" type="x-p"/> That this is the case is evident from <reference osisRef="Isa.24.4-Isa.24.9">Isa 24:4-9</reference>, where the accursed state into which the earth is brought is more fully described, and the cause thereof is given. <hi type="italic">“Smitten down, withered up is the earth; pined away, wasted away is the world; pined away have they, the foremost of the people of the earth. And the earth has become wicked among its inhabitants; for they transgressed revelations, set at nought the ordinance, broke the everlasting covenant. Therefore hath the curse devoured the earth, and they who dwelt in it make expiation: therefore are the inhabitants of the earth withered up, and there are very few mortals left. New wine mourneth, vine is parched, all the merry-hearted groan. The joyous playing of tabrets is silent; the noise of them that rejoice hath ceased; the joyous playing of the guitar is silent. They drink no wine with a song; meth tastes bitter to them that drink it.”</hi> “The world” (<hi type="italic">tēbēl</hi>) is used here in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.4">Isa 24:4</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Isa 26:9</reference> (always in the form of a proper name, and without the article), as a parallel to “<hi type="italic">the earth</hi>” (<hi type="italic">hâ'âretz</hi>), with which it alternates throughout this cycle of prophecies. It is used poetically to signify the globe, and that without limitation (even in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Isa 13:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.18.3">Isa 18:3</reference>); and therefore “the earth” is also to be understood here in its most comprehensive sense (in a different sense, therefore, from <reference osisRef="Isa.33.9">Isa 33:9</reference>, which contains the same play upon sounds). The earth is sunk in mourning, and has become like a faded plant, withered up with heat; the high ones of the people of the earth (<hi type="italic">merōm</hi>; <hi type="italic">abstr. pro concr.</hi>, like <hi type="italic">câbōd</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.13">Isa 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.24">Isa 22:24</reference>) are included (עם is used, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.42.5">Isa 42:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.7">Isa 40:7</reference>, to signify humanity, i.e., man generally). אמללוּ (for the form, see <hi type="italic">Comm. on Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Job.18.16-Job.18.19">Job 18:16-19</reference>) stands in half pause, which throws the subjective notion that follows into greater prominence. It is the punishment of the inhabitants of the earth, which the earth has to share, because it has shared in the wickedness of those who live upon it: <hi type="italic">chânaph</hi> (not related to <hi type="italic">tânaph</hi>) signifies to be degenerate, to have decided for what is evil (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.16">Isa 9:16</reference>), to be wicked; and in this intransitive sense it is applied to the land, which is said to be affected with the guilt of wicked, reckless conduct, more especially of blood-guiltiness (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.38">Psa 106:38</reference>; Num 35:33; compare the transitive use in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.9">Jer 3:9</reference>). The wicked conduct of men, which has caused the earth also to become <hi type="italic">chanēphâh</hi>, is described in three short, rapid, involuntarily excited sentences (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.15.6">Isa 15:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.4">Isa 16:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.20">Isa 29:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.8">Isa 33:8</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Isa.24.5">Isa 24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Isa 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Isa 1:8</reference>; out of the book of Isaiah, however, we only meet with this in <reference osisRef="Joel.1.10">Joe 1:10</reference>, and possibly <reference osisRef="Josh.7.11">Jos 7:11</reference>). Understanding “the earth” as we do in a general sense, “the law” cannot signify merely the positive law of Israel. The Gentile world had also a <hi type="italic">torâh</hi> or divine teaching within, which contained an abundance of divine directions (<hi type="italic">tōrōth</hi>). They also had a law written in their hearts; and it was with the whole human race that God concluded a covenant in the person of Noah, at a time when the nations had none of them come into existence at all. This is the explanation given by even Jewish commentators; nevertheless, we must not forget that Israel was included among the transgressors, and the choice of expression was determined by this. With the expression “therefore” the prophecy moves on from sin to punishment, just as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Isa 5:25</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference>). אלה is the curse of God denounced against the transgressors of His law (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.11">Dan 9:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.23.10">Jer 23:10</reference>, which is founded upon this, and from which אבלה has been introduced into this passage in some codices and editions). The curse of God devours, for it is fire, and that from within outwards (see <reference osisRef="Isa.1.31">Isa 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.18">Isa 9:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16-Isa.10.17">Isa 10:16-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Isa 29:6</reference>; Isa 30:27., <reference osisRef="Isa.33.11-Isa.33.14">Isa 33:11-14</reference>): <hi type="italic">chârū</hi> (<hi type="italic">milel</hi>, since <hi type="italic">pashta</hi> is an <hi type="italic">acc. postpos.</hi>),<note placement="foot">In correct texts <hi type="italic">châr</hi> has two <hi type="italic">pashtas</hi>, the former indicating the place of the tone.</note> from <hi type="italic">chârar</hi>, they are burnt up, <hi type="italic">exusti</hi>. With regard to ויּאשׁמוּ, it is hardly necessary to observe that it cannot be traced back to אשׁם = ישׁם, שׁמם; and that of the two meanings, <hi type="italic">culpam contrahere</hi> and <hi type="italic">culpam sustinere</hi>, it has the latter meaning here. We must not overlook the genuine mark of Isaiah here in the description of the vanishing away of men down to a small remnant: נשׁאר (שׁאר) is the standing word used to denote this; מזער (used with regard to number both here and in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Isa 16:14</reference>; and with regard to time in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.25">Isa 10:25</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.29.17">Isa 29:17</reference>) is exclusively Isaiah's; and אנושׁ is used in the same sense as in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.8">Isa 33:8</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.13.12">Isa 13:12</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Isa.24.7">Isa 24:7</reference> we are reminded of Joel 1 (on the short sentences, see <reference osisRef="Isa.29.20">Isa 29:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8-Isa.16.10">Isa 16:8-10</reference>); in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.8">Isa 24:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.9">Isa 24:9</reference> any one acquainted with Isaiah’s style will recall to mind not only <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa 5:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference>, but a multitude of other parallels. We content ourselves with pointing to עלּיז (which belongs exclusively to Isaiah, and is taken from <reference osisRef="Isa.22.2">Isa 22:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Isa 32:13</reference> in Zep 2:15, and from <reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Isa 13:3</reference> in Zep 3:11); and for <hi type="italic">basshir</hi> (with joyous song) to <reference osisRef="Isa.30.32">Isa 30:32</reference> (with the beating of drums and playing of guitars), together with Isa 28:7. The picture is elegiac, and dwells so long upon the wine (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1-Isa.16.14">Isa 16:1-14</reference>), just because wine, both as a natural production and in the form of drink, is the most exhilarating to the heart of all the natural gifts of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.15">Psa 104:15</reference>; Jdg 9:13). All the sources of joy and gladness are destroyed; and even if there is much still left of that which ought to give enjoyment, the taste of the men themselves turns it into bitterness.
entries.e6b344000166d360d2550a0001b55a2224b6ac0c: <reference osisRef="Isa.24.10-Isa.24.13">Isa 24:10-13</reference> <div eID="gen13125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13126" type="x-p"/> The world with its pleasure is judged; the world’s city is also judged, in which both the world’s power and the world’s pleasure were concentrated. <hi type="italic">“The city of tohu is broken to pieces; every house is shut up, so that no man can come in. There is lamentation for wine in the fields; all rejoicing has set; the delight of the earth is banished. What is left of the city is wilderness, and the gate was shattered to ruins. For so will it be within the earth, in the midst of the nations; as at the olive-beating, as at the gleaning, when the vintage is over.”</hi> The city of <hi type="italic">tohu</hi> (<hi type="italic">kiryath</hi> <hi type="italic">tōhu</hi>): this cannot be taken collectively, as Rosenmüller, Arndt, and Drechsler suppose, on account of the annexation of <hi type="italic">kiryath</hi> to <hi type="italic">tohu</hi>, which is turned into a kind of proper name; for can we understand it as referring to Jerusalem, as the majority of commentators have done, including even Schegg and Stier (according to <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13-Isa.32.14">Isa 32:13-14</reference>), after we have taken “the earth” (<hi type="italic">hâ'âretz</hi>) in the sense of <hi type="italic">kosmos</hi> (the world). It is rather the central city of the world as estranged from God; and it is here designated according to its end, which end will be <hi type="italic">tohu</hi>, as its nature was <hi type="italic">tohu</hi>. Its true nature was the breaking up of the harmony of all divine order; and so its end will be the breaking up of its own standing, and a hurling back, as it were, into the <hi type="italic">chaos</hi> of its primeval beginning. With a very similar significance Rome is called <hi type="italic">turbida Roma</hi> in Persius (i. 5). The whole is thoroughly Isaiah’s, even to the finest points: <hi type="italic">tohu</hi> is the same as in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Isa 29:21</reference>; and for the expression מבּוא (so that you cannot enter; namely, on account of the ruins which block up the doorway) compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1">Isa 23:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">Isa 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa 17:1</reference>, also <reference osisRef="Isa.5.9">Isa 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.11">Isa 6:11</reference>; Isa 32:13. The cry or lamentation for the wine out in the fields (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.11">Isa 24:11</reference>; cf., <reference osisRef="Job.5.10">Job 5:10</reference>) is the mourning on account of the destruction of the vineyards; the vine, which is one of Isaiah’s most favourite symbols, represents in this instance also all the natural sources of joy. In the term <hi type="italic">‛ârbâh</hi> (rejoicing) the relation between joy and light is presupposed; the sun of joy is set (compare Mic 3:6). What remains of the city בּעיר is partitive, just as בּו in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa 10:22</reference>) is <hi type="italic">shammâh</hi> (desolation), to which the whole city has been brought (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.5.9">Isa 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.14">Isa 32:14</reference>). The strong gates, which once swarmed with men, are shattered to ruins (<hi type="italic">yuccath</hi>, like Mic 1:7, for <hi type="italic">yūcath</hi>, Ges. §§67, Anm. 8; שׁאיּה, ἁπ λεγ, a predicating noun of sequence, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Isa 37:26</reference>, “into desolated heaps;” compare <reference osisRef="Isa.6.11">Isa 6:11</reference>, etc., and other passages). In the whole circuit of the earth (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.12">Isa 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.7.22">Isa 7:22</reference>; <hi type="italic">hâ'âretz</hi> is “the earth” here as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.23">Isa 10:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.24">Isa 19:24</reference>), and in the midst of what was once a crowd of nations (compare Mic 5:6-7), there is only a small remnant of men left. This is the leading thought, which runs through the book of Isaiah from beginning to end, and is figuratively depicted here in a miniature of <reference osisRef="Isa.17.4">Isa 17:4</reference>-6. The state of things produced by the catastrophe is compared to the olive-beating, which fetches down what fruit was left at the general picking, and to the gleaning of the grapes after the vintage has been fully gathered in (<hi type="italic">câlâh</hi> is used here as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.25">Isa 10:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.4">Isa 16:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.16">Isa 21:16</reference>, etc., viz., “to be over,” whereas in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.10">Isa 32:10</reference> it means to be hopelessly lost, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.6">Isa 15:6</reference>). There are no more men in the whole of the wide world than there are of olives and grapes after the principal gathering has taken place. The persons saved belong chiefly, though not exclusively, to Israel (Joh 3:5). The place where they assemble is the land of promise.
entries.0535e6241a0344f3c9e184576216edb41b90f743: <reference osisRef="Isa.24.14-Isa.24.15">Isa 24:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen13126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13127" type="x-p"/> There is now a church there refined by the judgment, and rejoicing in its apostolic calling to the whole world. <hi type="italic">“They will lift up their voice, and exult; for the majesty of Jehovah they shout from the sea: therefore praise ye Jehovah in the lands of the sun, in the islands of the sea the name of Jehovah the God of Israel.”</hi> The ground and subject of the rejoicing is “the majesty of Jehovah,” i.e., the fact that Jehovah had shown Himself so majestic in judgment and mercy (<reference osisRef="Isa.12.5-Isa.12.6">Isa 12:5-6</reference>), and was now so manifest in His glory (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Isa 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.17">Isa 2:17</reference>). Therefore rejoicing was heard “from the sea” (the Mediterranean), by which the abode of the congregation of Jehovah was washed. Turning in that direction, it had the islands and coast lands of the European West in front (<hi type="italic">iyyi</hi> <hi type="italic">hayyâm</hi>; the only other passage in which this occurs is <reference osisRef="Isa.11.11">Isa 11:11</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.18">Eze 26:18</reference>), and at its back the lands of the Asiatic East, which are called <hi type="italic">'urim</hi>, the lands of light, i.e., of the sun-rising. This is the true meaning of <hi type="italic">'urim</hi>, as J. Schelling and Drechsler agree; for Döderlein’s comparison of the rare Arabic word <hi type="italic">awr</hi>, <hi type="italic">septentrio</hi> is as far removed from the Hebrew usage as that of the Talmud אור אורתּא, <hi type="italic">vespera</hi>. Hitzig’s proposed reading באיים (according to the lxx) diminishes the substance and destroys the beauty of the appeal, which goes forth both to the east and west, and summons to the praise of the name of Jehovah the God of Israel, על־כּן, i.e., because of His manifested glory. His “name” (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27">Isa 30:27</reference>) is His nature as revealed and made “nameable” in judgment and mercy.
entries.44c4009513e0ede17891c455e0415ac99abdeb7e: <reference osisRef="Isa.24.16-Isa.24.20">Isa 24:16-20</reference> <div eID="gen13127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13128" type="x-p"/> This appeal is not made in vain. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.24.16">Isa 24:16</reference></hi>. <hi type="italic">“From the border of the earth we hear songs: Praise to the Righteous One!”</hi> It no doubt seems natural enough to understand the term <hi type="italic">tzaddı̄k</hi> (righteous) as referring to Jehovah; but, as Hitzig observes, Jehovah is never called “the Righteous One” in so absolute a manner as this (compare, however, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">Psa 112:4</reference>, where it occurs in connection with other attributes, and <reference osisRef="Exod.9.27">Exo 9:27</reference>, where it stands in an antithetical relation); and in addition to this, Jehovah gives צבי (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Isa 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.5">Isa 28:5</reference>), whilst כבוד, and not צבי, is ascribed to Him. Hence we must take the word in the same sense as in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10">Isa 3:10</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Hab 2:4</reference>). The reference is to the church of righteous men, whose faith has endured the fire of the judgment of wrath. In response to its summons to the praise of Jehovah, they answer it in songs from the border of the earth. The earth is here thought of as a garment spread out; <hi type="italic">cenaph</hi> is the point or edge of the garment, the extreme eastern and western ends (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Isa 11:12</reference>). Thence the church of the future catches the sound of this grateful song as it is echoed from one to the other. <div eID="gen13128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13129" type="x-p"/> The prophet feels himself, “in spirit,” to be a member of this church; but all at once he becomes aware of the sufferings which will have first of all to be overcome, and which he cannot look upon without sharing the suffering himself. <hi type="italic">“Then I said, Ruin to me! ruin to me! Woe to me! Robbers rob, and robbing, they rob as robbers. Horror, and pit, and snare, are over thee, O inhabitant of the earth! And it cometh to pass, whoever fleeth from the tidings of horror falleth into the pit; and whoever escapeth out of the pit is caught in the snare: for the trap-doors on high are opened, and the firm foundations of the earth shake. The earth rending, is rent asunder; the earth bursting, is burst in pieces; the earth shaking, tottereth. The earth reeling, reeleth like a drunken man, and swingeth like a hammock; and its burden of sin presseth upon it; and it falleth, and riseth not again.”</hi> The expression “Then I said” (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.6.5">Isa 6:5</reference>) stands here in the same apocalyptic connection as in <reference osisRef="Rev.7.14">Rev 7:14</reference>, for example. He said it at that time in a state of ecstasy; so that when he committed to writing what he had seen, the saying was a thing of the past. The final salvation follows a final judgment; and looking back upon the latter, he bursts out into the exclamation of pain: <hi type="italic">râzı̄</hi>-<hi type="italic">lı̄</hi>, consumption, passing away, to me (see <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">Isa 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.4">Isa 17:4</reference>), i.e., I must perish (<hi type="italic">râzi</hi> is a word of the same form as <hi type="italic">kâli</hi>, <hi type="italic">shâni</hi>, <hi type="italic">‛âni</hi>; literally, it is a neuter adjective signifying <hi type="italic">emaciatum</hi> = <hi type="italic">macies</hi>; Ewald, §749,<hi type="italic">g</hi>). He sees a dreadful, bloodthirsty people preying among both men and stores (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">Isa 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa 33:1</reference>, for the play upon the word with בגד, root גד, cf., κεύθειν τινά τι, <hi type="italic">tecte agere</hi>, i.e., from behind, treacherously, like assassins). The exclamation, “Horror, and pit,” etc. (which Jeremiah applies in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.43-Jer.48.44">Jer 48:43-44</reference>, to the destruction of Moab by the Chaldeans), is not an invocation, but simply a deeply agitated utterance of what is inevitable. In the pit and snare there is a comparison implied of men to game, and of the enemy to sportsmen (cf., <reference osisRef="Jer.15.16">Jer 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.19">Lam 4:19</reference>; <hi type="italic">yillâcēr</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.15">Isa 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.13">Isa 28:13</reference>). The על in עליך is exactly the same as in Jdg 16:9 (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Isa 16:9</reference>). They who should flee as soon as the horrible news arrived (<hi type="italic">min</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.3">Isa 33:3</reference>) would not escape destruction, but would become victims to one form if not to another (the same thought which we find expressed twice in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.19">Amo 5:19</reference>, and still more fully in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1-Isa.9.4">Isa 9:1-4</reference>, as well as in a more dreadfully exalted tone). Observe, however, in how mysterious a background those human instruments of punishment remain, who are suggested by the word <hi type="italic">bōgdim</hi> (robbers). The idea that the judgment is a direct act of Jehovah, stands in the foreground and governs the whole. For this reason it is described as a repetition of the flood (for the opened windows or trap-doors of the firmament, which let the great bodies of water above them come down from on high upon the earth, point back to <reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Gen 7:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.8.2">Gen 8:2</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.78.23">Psa 78:23</reference>); and this indirectly implies its universality. It is also described as an earthquake. “The foundations of the earth” are the internal supports upon which the visible crust of the earth rests. The way in which the earth in its quaking first breaks, then bursts, and then falls, is painted for the ear by the three reflective forms in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.19">Isa 24:19</reference>, together with their gerundives, which keep each stage in the process of the catastrophe vividly before the mind. רעה is apparently an error of the pen for רע, if it is not indeed a <hi type="italic">n. actionis</hi> instead of the <hi type="italic">inf. absol.</hi> as in Hab 3:9. The accentuation, however, regards the <hi type="italic">ah</hi> as a toneless addition, and the form therefore as a gerundive (like <hi type="italic">kob</hi> in Num 23:25). The reflective form התרעע is not the <hi type="italic">hithpalel</hi> of רוּע, <hi type="italic">vociferari</hi>, but the <hi type="italic">hithpoel</hi> of רעע (רצץ), <hi type="italic">frangere</hi>. The threefold play upon the words would be tame, if the words themselves formed an anti-climax; but it is really a <hi type="italic">climax ascendens</hi>. The earth first of all receives rents; then gaping wide, it bursts asunder; and finally sways to and fro once more, and falls. It is no longer possible for it to keep upright. Its wickedness presses it down like a burden (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.5">Psa 38:5</reference>), so that it now reels for the last time like a drunken man (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Isa 28:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9">Isa 29:9</reference>), or a hammock (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Isa 1:8</reference>), until it falls never to rise again.
entries.d8fab5471f64be9a227220d4a0df59110966a8fa: <reference osisRef="Isa.24.21">Isa 24:21</reference> <div eID="gen13129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13130" type="x-p"/> But if the old earth passes away in this manner out of the system of the universe, the punishment of God must fall at the same time both upon the princes of heaven and upon the princes of earth (the prophet does not arrange what belongs to the end of all things in a “chronotactic” manner). They are the secrets of two worlds, that are here unveiled to the apocalyptic seer of the Old Testament. <hi type="italic">“And it cometh to pass in that day, Jehovah will visit the army of the high place in the high place, and the kings of the earth on the earth. And they are imprisoned, as one imprisons captives in the pit, and shut up in prison; and in the course of many days they are visited. And the moon blushes, and the sun turns pale: for Jehovah of hosts reigns royally upon Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and before His elders is glory.”</hi> With this doubly expressed antithesis of <hi type="italic">mârōm</hi> and <hi type="italic">'adâmâh</hi> (cf., <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.23.17">Isa 23:17</reference></hi>) before us, brought out as it is as sharply as possible, we cannot understand “<hi type="italic">the army of the high place</hi>” as referring to certain earthly powers (as the Targum, Luther, Calvin, and Hävernick do). Moreover, the expression itself is also opposed to such an interpretation; for, as <reference osisRef="Isa.24.18">Isa 24:18</reference> clearly shows, in which <hi type="italic">mimmârom</hi> is equivalent to <hi type="italic">misshâmaim</hi> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.33.5">Isa 33:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.23">Isa 37:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.26">Isa 40:26</reference>), מרום צבא is synonymous with השּׁמים צבא; and this invariably signifies either the starry host (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.26">Isa 40:26</reference>) or the angelic host (1Ki 22:19; <reference osisRef="Ps.148.2">Psa 148:2</reference>), and occasionally the two combined, without any distinction (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.6">Neh 9:6</reference>). As the moon and sun are mentioned, it might be supposed that by the “host on high” we are to understand the angelic host, as Abravanel, Umbreit, and others really do: “the stars, that have been made into idols, the shining kings of the sky, fall from their altars, and the kings of the earth from their thrones.” But the very antithesis in the word “kings” (<hi type="italic">malchē</hi>) leads us to conjecture that “the host on high” refers to personal powers; and the view referred to founders on the more minute description of the visitation (<hi type="italic">pâkad</hi> <hi type="italic">‛al</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">Isa 27:3</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Isa 26:21</reference>), “they are imprisoned,” etc.; for this must also be referred to the heavenly host. The objection might indeed be urged, that the imprisonment only relates to the kings, and that the visitation of the heavenly host finds its full expression in the shaming of the moon and sun (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa 24:23</reference>); but the fact that the moon and sun are thrown into the shade by the revelation of the glory of Jehovah, cannot be regarded as a judgment inflicted upon them. Hence the commentators are now pretty well agreed, that “the host on high” signifies here the angelic army. But it is self-evident, that a visitation of the angelic army cannot be merely a relative and partial one. And it is not sufficient to understand the passage as meaning the wicked angels, to the exclusion of the good. Both the context and the parallelism show that the reference must be to a penal visitation in the spiritual world, which stands in the closest connection with the history of man, and in fact with the history of the nations. Consequently the host on high will refer to the angels of the nations and kingdoms; and the prophecy here presupposes what is affirmed in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.8">Deu 32:8</reference> (lxx), and sustained in the book of Daniel, when it speaks of a <hi type="italic">sar</hi> of Persia, Javan, and even the people of Israel. In accordance with this exposition, there is a rabbinical saying, to the effect that “God never destroys a nation without having first of all destroyed its prince,” i.e., the angel who, by whatever means he first obtained possession of the nation, whether by the will of God or against His will, has exerted an ungodly influence upon it. Just as, according to the scriptural view, both good and evil angels attach themselves to particular men, and an elevated state of mind may sometimes afford a glimpse of this encircling company and this conflict of spirits; so do angels contend for the rule over nations and kingdoms, either to guide them in the way of God or to lead them astray from God; and therefore the judgment upon the nations which the prophet here foretells will be a judgment upon angels also. The kingdom of spirits has its own history running parallel to the destinies of men. What is recorded in Gen 6 was a seduction of men by angels, and one of later occurrence than the temptation by Satan in paradise; and the seduction of nations and kingdoms by the host of heaven, which is here presupposed by the prophecy of Isaiah, is later than either.
entries.39db5c82a118796145e17ba4c1b74849a5b34b54: <reference osisRef="Isa.24.22-Isa.24.23">Isa 24:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen13130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13131" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.24.22">Isa 24:22</reference> announces the preliminary punishment of both angelic and human princes: <hi type="italic">'asēphâh</hi> stands in the place of a gerundive, like <hi type="italic">taltēlâh</hi> in Isa 22:17. The connection of the words <hi type="italic">'asēphâh 'assir</hi> is exactly the same as that of <hi type="italic">taltēlâh</hi> <hi type="italic">gâbēr</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.17">Isa 22:17</reference> : incarceration after the manner of incarcerating prisoners; <hi type="italic">'âsaph</hi>, to gather together (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.14">Isa 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.4">Isa 33:4</reference>), signifies here to incarcerate, just as in Gen 42:17. Both verbs are construed with <hi type="italic">‛al</hi>, because the thrusting is from above downwards, into the pit and prison (<hi type="italic">‛al</hi> embraces both <hi type="italic">upon</hi> or <hi type="italic">over</hi> anything, and <hi type="italic">into</hi> it, e.g., <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.4">1Sa 31:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.6.16">Job 6:16</reference>; see Hitzig on <reference osisRef="Nah.3.12">Nah 3:12</reference>). We may see from 2Pe 2:4 and <reference osisRef="Jude.1.6">Jud 1:6</reference> how this is to be understood. The reference is to the abyss of Hades, where they are reserved in chains of darkness unto the judgment of the great day. According to this parallel, <hi type="italic">yippâkedu</hi> (shall be visited) ought apparently to be understood as denoting a visitation in wrath (like <reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Isa 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.8">Eze 38:8</reference>; compare <hi type="italic">pâkad</hi> followed by an accusative in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Isa 26:21</reference>, also <reference osisRef="Isa.26.14">Isa 26:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.59.6">Psa 59:6</reference>; <hi type="italic">niphkad</hi>, in fact, is never used to signify visitation in mercy), and therefore as referring to the infliction of the final punishment. Hitzig, however, understands it as relating to a visitation of mercy; and in this he is supported by Ewald, Knobel, and Luzzatto. Gesenius, Umbreit, and others, take it to indicate a citation or summons, though without any ground either in usage of speech or actual custom. A comparison of <reference osisRef="Isa.23.17">Isa 23:17</reference> in its relation to <reference osisRef="Isa.23.15">Isa 23:15</reference><note placement="foot">Cf., Targ., Saad., “they will come into remembrance again.”</note> favours the second explanation, as being relatively the most correct; but the expression is intentionally left ambiguous. So far as the thing itself is concerned, we have a parallel in <reference osisRef="Rev.20.1-Rev.20.3">Rev 20:1-3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Rev.20.7-Rev.20.9">Rev 20:7-9</reference> : they are visited by being set free again, and commencing their old practice once more; but only (as <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa 24:23</reference> affirms) to lose again directly, before the glorious and triumphant might of Jehovah, the power they have temporarily reacquired. What the apocalyptist of the New Testament describes in detail in <reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">Rev 20:4</reference>, Rev 20:11., and <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Rev 21:1</reference>, the apocalyptist of the Old Testament sees here condensed into one fact, viz., the enthroning of Jehovah and His people in a new Jerusalem, at which the silvery white moon (<hi type="italic">lebânâh</hi>) turns red, and the glowing sun (<hi type="italic">chammâh</hi>) turns pale; the two great lights of heaven becoming (according to a Jewish expression) “like a lamp at noonday” in the presence of such glory. Of the many parallels to <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa 24:23</reference> which we meet with in Isaiah, the most worthy of note are <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">Isa 11:10</reference> to the concluding clause, “and before His elders is glory” (also <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa 4:5</reference>), and <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Isa 1:26</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.3.14">Isa 3:14</reference>), with reference to the use of the word <hi type="italic">zekēnim</hi> (elders). Other parallels are <reference osisRef="Isa.30.26">Isa 30:26</reference>, for <hi type="italic">chammâh</hi> and <hi type="italic">lebânâh</hi>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference>, for <hi type="italic">châphēr</hi> and <hi type="italic">bōsh</hi>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.22">Isa 33:22</reference>, for <hi type="italic">mâlak</hi>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Isa 10:12</reference>, for “Mount Zion and Jerusalem.” We have already spoken at <reference osisRef="Isa.1.16">Isa 1:16</reference> of the word neged (Arab. <hi type="italic">Ne'gd</hi>, from <hi type="italic">nâgad</hi>, <hi type="italic">njd</hi>, to be exalted; vid., opp. Arab. <hi type="italic">gâr</hi>, to be pressed down, to sink), as applied to that which stands out prominently and clearly before one’s eyes. According to Hofmann (<hi type="italic">Schriftbeweis</hi>, i. 320-1), the elders here, like the twenty-four <hi type="italic">presbuteroi</hi> of the Apocalypse, are the sacred spirits, forming the council of God, to which He makes known His will concerning the world, before it is executed by His attendant spirits the angels. But as we find counsellors promised to the Israel of the new Jerusalem in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Isa 1:26</reference>, in contrast with the bad <hi type="italic">zekēnim</hi> (elders) which it then possessed (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.14">Isa 3:14</reference>), such as it had at the glorious commencement of its history; and as the passage before us says essentially the same with regard to the <hi type="italic">zekēnim</hi> as we find in <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa 4:5</reference> with regard to the festal meetings of Israel (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.30.20">Isa 30:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Isa 32:1</reference>); and still further, as <reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">Rev 20:4</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mat 19:28</reference>) is a more appropriate parallel to the passage before us than <reference osisRef="Rev.4.4">Rev 4:4</reference>, we may assume with certainty, at least with regard to this passage, and without needing to come to any decision concerning <reference osisRef="Rev.4.4">Rev 4:4</reference>, that the <hi type="italic">zekēnim</hi> here are not angels, but human elders after God’s own heart. These elders, being admitted into the immediate presence of God, and reigning together with Him, have nothing but glory in front of them, and they themselves reflect that glory. The Fourfold Melodious Echo - Isaiah 25-26 <div eID="gen13131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13132" type="x-p"/> A. First Echo - <reference osisRef="Isa.25.1-Isa.25.8">Isa 25:1-8</reference> <div eID="gen13132" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Salvation of the Nations after the Fall of the Imperial City</title> <div sID="gen13133" type="x-p"/> There is not merely reflected glory, but reflected sound as well. The melodious echoes commence with Isa 25:1. The prophet, transported to the end of the days, commemorates what he has seen in psalms and songs. These psalms and songs not only repeat what has already been predicted; but, sinking into it, and drawing out of it, they partly expand it themselves, and partly prepare the way for its further extension.  <chapter eID="Isa.24"/> <div eID="gen13133" type="x-p"/>

entries.c145e9e32593adf96dde397e0f8fd939e4e60ed6: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.1" sID="gen44171" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Behold, Jehovah maketh the earth empty.</hi> This prophecy, so far as I can judge, is the conclusion of all the descriptions that have been given from the thirteenth chapter downwards, in which Isaiah foretold destruction not only to the Jews and to Israel, but to the Moabites, Assyrians, Egyptians, and other nations. In short, having, as it were, surveyed all the countries which were near the Jews and known to them, he gives a brief summary of the whole. Some view this as referring to Israel, and others to the Jews, and think that their destruction is foretold; but as he mentions <hi type="italic">the world</hi>, I can view it in no other light than as a comprehensive statement of all that he formerly said about each of them, and at different times. Nor is this view contradicted by the fact that he immediately mentions <hi type="italic">the priest</hi>, which might lead us to believe that these things relate to none but the people of God; for although he speaks of all the nations, yet because the Jews always hold the highest rank, Isaiah must have had them especially in his eye, for he was appointed to them. It may be said to have been accidental that he mentions other nations; and therefore we ought not to wonder if, after having made reference to them, he speaks particularly about his own people in a single word.<div eID="gen44172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44173" type="x-p"/>Others suppose that he means “the whole world,” but think that he refers to the last day, which I consider to be an excessively forced interpretation; for, after having threatened the Jews and other nations, the Prophet afterwards adds a consolation, that the Lord will one day raise up his Church and make her more flourishing; which certainly cannot apply to the last judgment. But by the term <hi type="italic">the earth</hi>, I do not think that the Prophet means the whole world, but the countries well known to the Jews; just as in the present day, when we speak of what happens in the world, we almost never go beyond Europe, or think of what is passing in India; for this may be said to be our world. Thus, Isaiah speaks of “the earth” known to himself and to all whom he addressed, and of the people who inhabited the neighboring countries. In short, we may limit the term “World” to the Egyptians, Assyrians, Moabites, Tyrians, and such like; as if he had said, “Hitherto I have spoken of various calamities, which threatened many nations, and still in part threaten some of them; but I may sum up all by saying, ‘The Lord will overturn and strip the face of the earth of all its ornaments.’”<div eID="gen44173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44174" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And maketh it bare.</hi> <note n="121"> <div sID="gen44175" type="x-p"/> “And maketh it waste.” — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen44175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44176" type="x-p"/> FT379 “The haughty people of the earth. (Heb. the height of the people.)” — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen44176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44177" type="x-p"/> FT380 “The earth also is defiled.” — Eng. Ver. “The earth is even polluted.” — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi>. “And the land has been profaned.” — <hi type="italic">Alexander</hi><div eID="gen44177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44178" type="x-p"/> FT381 “On account of the sin of perjury is the earth consumed.” — <hi type="italic">Jarchi</hi>. “<foreign xml:lang="he">אלה</foreign> (ā<hi type="italic">lāh</hi>) does not here mean false swearing, as explained in the Targum, and by Jarchi, and Kimchi, but the curse of God attending the violation of his law.” — <hi type="italic">Alexander</hi><div eID="gen44178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44179" type="x-p"/> FT382 “<foreign xml:lang="he">אשם</foreign> (ā<hi type="italic">shăm</hi>) is taken by some of the early writers in the sense of being <hi type="italic">desolate</hi>. Its true sense is that of being recognised as guilty, and treated accordingly. It therefore suggests the ideas both of guilt and punishment.” — <hi type="italic">Alexander</hi><div eID="gen44179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44180" type="x-p"/> FT383 “The city of confusion.” — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen44180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44181" type="x-p"/> FT384 “In the fires, (or, valleys.)” — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen44181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44182" type="x-p"/> FT385 “The uttermost part. (Heb. wing.)” — Eng. Ver. The Septuagint translates it literally, <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀπὸ τῶν πτερύγων τὢς γὢς</foreign>, “from the wings of the earth” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen44182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44183" type="x-p"/> FT386 There is a considerable diversity of opinion about the application of the term <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> in this passage. Many commentators agree with Calvin in thinking that God is here called <hi type="italic">righteous</hi>. Bishop Stock has slightly modified this view by applying the designation to the Messiah. “By the righteous,” says he, “is probably meant one person the Messiah, (see <reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.52 Bible:Acts.22.14">Acts 7:52, 22:14</reference>,) whose kingdom the Prophet beholds in vision, and joins in the chorus of joy at its approach; a joy, however, which is presently interrupted by a reflection on the wickedness of the greater part of his countrymen at that time, who should reject the Lord that bought them. Therefore he saith, Woe is me! destruction shall overtake the inhabitants of the land.” Instead of “Glory to the righteous,” the Septuagint renders it, <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐλπὶς τῶ εὐσεβεῖ</foreign>, “hope to the godly man.” Professor Alexander’s rendering is, “Praise to the righteous;” and he remarks, <foreign xml:lang="he">צדיק</foreign> (<hi type="italic">tzăddīk</hi>) is not an epithet of God (Henderson) or Cyrus (Hendewerk), but of righteous men in general.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen44183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44184" type="x-p"/> FT387 “My leanness. (Heb. leanness to me, or, my secret to me.)” — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen44184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44185" type="x-p"/> FT388 “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Nous n’avons raison aucune d’accuser celuy qui nous frappe</foreign>;” — “We have no reason to blame him who strikes us.”<div eID="gen44185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44186" type="x-p"/> FT389 “Interpreters have commonly assumed that ‘the host of the high place’ is the same with the ‘host of heaven,’ and must therefore mean either stars (Jerome), or angels (Aben Ezra), or both (Gesenius). Grotius understands by it the images of the heavenly bodies worshipped in Assyria. Gesenius finds here an allusion to the punishment of fallen angels, and then makes this a proof of recent origin, because the Jewish demonology was later than the time of Isaiah. It may be doubted whether there is any reference to the hosts of heaven at all.” — <hi type="italic">Alexander</hi><div eID="gen44186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44187" type="x-p"/> FT390 “The Lord shall punish (Heb. visit upon) the host of the high ones.” — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen44187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44188" type="x-p"/> FT391 “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Des enfans de Dieu</foreign>;” — “Of the children of God.”<div eID="gen44188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44189" type="x-p"/> FT392 “And before his ancients gloriously; (or, there shall be glory before his ancients.)” — Eng. Ver. “Before his ancients shall he be glorified.” — <hi type="italic">Lowth</hi>. “And before his elders shall there be glory.” — <hi type="italic">Alexander</hi><div eID="gen44189" type="x-p"/> </note> Some translate <foreign xml:lang="he">בלקה</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">bōlĕkāch</hi>,) <hi type="italic">he uncovereth the earth,</hi> that the enemies may have free entrance into it. But I choose rather to translate it, “he maketh bare the earth,” because the earth is said to be “covered,” when it is inhabited by a great multitude of men, and when it abounds in fruits and flocks; and it is said to be “uncovered” or “laid bare,” when it is deprived of its inhabitants, and when its covering is taken away from it, as if one were stripped of his raiment and ornaments. Now, this must have happened not only to the Jews, but to the Assyrians, Egyptians, and other nations, which he had mentioned; and therefore to all of them together he threatens their ruin.<div eID="gen44174" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44171" osisID="Isa.24.1" type="section"/>
entries.637fcbd8928503981b56d974896622cfa8bdc655: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.2" sID="gen44190" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">And it shall be.</hi> By these words he means the utmost desolation, in which there will be no longer any distinction of ranks or any appearance of a commonwealth; for so long as there is a tolerably regular form of government, some distinction continues to be maintained between “the people” and “the priests.” By a figure of speech, in which a part is taken for the whole, (<foreign xml:lang="el">συνεκδοχικῶς</foreign>,) he mentions one department instead of the whole class, as is frequently done in the Scriptures; though we might take <foreign xml:lang="he">כחנים</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">kōchănīm</hi>,) to mean those who hold any high rank; for Hebrew writers frequently give this name to princes, and especially to those who are of royal blood; but I have no reluctance to view it as an instance of the figure of speech which I have mentioned.<div eID="gen44191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44192" type="x-p"/>Since Isaiah reckons this confusion among the curses of God, and declares that, when the distinction of ranks is laid aside, it is a terrible display of the vengeance of God, we ought to conclude, on the other hand, how much God is pleased with regular government and the good order of society, and also how great a privilege it is to have it preserved among us; for when it is taken away, the life of man differs little from the sustenance of cattle and of beasts of prey. We ought therefore not only to acknowledge the dreadful vengeance of God, but also to lay it to the blame of our own sins, whenever he breaks down order and takes away instruction and courts of law; for when these fall, civilisation itself falls along with them. It ought also to be considered that, when the Lord executes his judgments, he spares no rank, not even the most sacred. What was this order of priests, which the Lord had so splendidly adorned, and had determined to consecrate to himself, and of which the people also boasted as if it had been unchangeable and eternal? Yet even the rank of priesthood is involved in the judgment of God, because there is no respect of persons, but, on the contrary, the more highly any have been favored, and the higher the rank to which they have been exalted, the more severely will he punish them, if they shall shew themselves to be ungrateful and abuse his benefits.<div eID="gen44192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44193" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">As the servant, so his master; as the buyer, so the seller.</hi> This statement is to the same effect with what goes before; for these ranks are manifestly lawful, and are not usually set aside, unless when the Lord determines to chastise his people with dreadful vengeance, as we have already said; for in a well-ordered society the distinction between master and servant must be observed. In like manner, no public government can be lasting without the transactions of commerce; and therefore, when the distinction between rich and poor has been taken away, every scheme for gaining a livelihood among men is destroyed. The meaning of the Prophet is, that all civil government will be broken up, because in such calamities, they who were the wealthiest are reduced to the lowest poverty. In short, he describes the most appalling desolation, which will be followed by unwonted change.<div eID="gen44193" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44190" osisID="Isa.24.2" type="section"/>
entries.cdc70f4fb068558a29f69dd2ef8a74b896d350cd: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.3" sID="gen44194" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">By emptying shall the earth be emptied.</hi> He confirms what he had already said, and declares that those changes will not be accidental, but that they are the work of God. In the first verse, he had expressly stated that God is making preparations for emptying the earth: he now asserts that it will happen, and adds the reason, that God hath purposed and determined to do it.<div eID="gen44195" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44194" osisID="Isa.24.3" type="section"/>
entries.57192cad660d13c5e499f823858707903664b0f4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.4" sID="gen44196" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44197" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> <hi type="italic">The earth hath lamented.</hi> Isaiah proceeds with his subject; for all this tends to explain the desolation of the whole world, that is, of the world which was known to the Jews. According to his custom, he illustrates the judgment of God more clearly by figures, which are fitted to produce an effect on sluggish minds.<div eID="gen44197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44198" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The lofty people of the earth.</hi> <note n="122"> <div sID="gen44199" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44199" type="x-p"/> </note> By the “lofty ones” we must understand those eminent persons who held a higher rank than others; for this is more wonderful than if the common people had fallen. Yet if it be thought preferable to explain it as relating peculiarly to the Jews, I have no objection; for although the Assyrians and Egyptians excelled them in wealth and power, still the Jews held the highest rank in this respect, that they had been adopted by God. But I prefer the other exposition, which makes the meaning to be, that the Lord would inflict punishment, not only on common people, but also on those who surpassed others in rank and splendor.<div eID="gen44198" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44196" osisID="Isa.24.4" type="section"/>
entries.46f920907228094dccc6d93c1ad5fcec28b8fbc4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.5" sID="gen44200" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44201" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the earth was deceitful.</hi> <note n="123"> <div sID="gen44202" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44202" type="x-p"/> </note> Others render it “defiled” or “polluted,” because <foreign xml:lang="he">כנף</foreign> (<hi type="italic">chānăph</hi>) means “to be wicked.” Both renderings may be appropriate; but the next verse appears to demand that we explain it to mean <hi type="italic">false</hi>; for he appears to illustrate and exhibit it more fully immediately afterwards, when he says that “the earth has been consumed by a curse.”<div eID="gen44201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44203" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Under its inhabitants.</hi> Whether <foreign xml:lang="he">תהת</foreign> (<hi type="italic">tăhăth</hi>) be translated “<hi type="italic">Under</hi> its inhabitants,” or, “<hi type="italic">On account of</hi> its inhabitants,” is of little importance. There is a kind of mutual bargain between the land and the husbandmen, that it gives back with usury what it has received: if it does not, it deceives those who cultivate it. But he assigns a reason, imputing blame to them, that they render it barren by their wickedness. It is owing to our fault that it does not nourish us or bring forth fruit, as God appointed to be done by the regular order of nature; for he wished that it should hold the place of a mother to us, to supply us with food; and if it change its nature and order, or lose its fertility, we ought to attribute it to our sins, since we ourselves have reversed the order which God had appointed; otherwise the earth would never deceive us, but would perform her duty.<div eID="gen44203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44204" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Because they have transgressed the laws.</hi> He immediately assigns the reason why the earth is unfaithful, and deceives her inhabitants. It is because those who refuse to honor God their Father and supporter, will justly be deprived of food and nourishment. Here he peculiarly holds up to shame the revolt of his nation, because it was baser and less excusable than all the transgressions of those who had never been taught in the school of God. The word <foreign xml:lang="he">תורה</foreign> (<hi type="italic">tōrāh</hi>) is applied to “the Law,” because it denotes instruction; but here, in the plural number, <foreign xml:lang="he">תורת</foreign> (<hi type="italic">tōrōth</hi>,) it denotes all the instruction that is contained in the “Law.” But as the “Law” contains both commandments and promises, he adds two parts for the purpose of explanation.<div eID="gen44204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44205" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">They have changed the ordinance.</hi> The Hebrew word <foreign xml:lang="he">חק</foreign> (<hi type="italic">chōk</hi>) means “an ordinance,” and on that account some think that it denotes ceremonies, and others that it denotes morals. We may render it “commandments;” and I understand it to mean not only ceremonies, but everything that belongs to the rule of a holy life.<div eID="gen44205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44206" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">They have broken the everlasting covenant.</hi> The third term employed by him is, <foreign xml:lang="he">ברית</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">bērīth</hi>,) by which he means a covenant and contract. This word is limited to those “contracts” by which the Lord, who adopted his people, promised that he would be their God. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.6 Bible:Exod.29.45">Exodus 19:6; 29:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.26.12">Leviticus 26:12</reference>.) He therefore charges them with ingratitude, because, when the Lord revealed himself by all these methods, and gave proofs of his love, they were disobedient and rebellious, “transgressed the laws,” and “broke the holy covenant.”<div eID="gen44206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44207" type="x-p"/>But why does he address himself to the Jews? Because he knew that he had been appointed to be their Prophet, that he might especially give instructions to them. Hence we may infer what is the rule of a holy life. It is contained in that law which we ought to follow if we wish that God should approve of our life; if we turn aside from it, we must be wicked and abandoned. We ought also to remark, that it is the will of God that in his word we should consider not only his commandments and laws, but also his covenant; for the chief part of the word consists of promises, by which he adopts and receives us as his own people. Besides, the Prophet unquestionably intended to use a variety of terms in order to express his meaning more strongly; as if he had said, “There is nothing about us that is sound and pure; everything is polluted and corrupted.”<div eID="gen44207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44208" type="x-p"/>He calls it “the covenant of eternity,” or “the everlasting covenant,” because it ought to be perpetual and inviolable, and to be in force in every age. It was to be transmitted, in uninterrupted succession, from father to son, that it might never be effaced from the memory of man, but might be kept pure and entire. He therefore represents in strong terms their treachery and wickedness, because they dared to violate that covenant which God had made with them, and to overthrow what the Lord intended to be firm and permanent. This was monstrous; and therefore we ought not to wonder that the earth takes vengeance for this wickedness, and refuses to give food to men.<div eID="gen44208" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44200" osisID="Isa.24.5" type="section"/>
entries.446fae9431bb7a762346cbc0892270768b7b8de7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.6" sID="gen44209" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi> <hi type="italic">Therefore hath the curse devoured the earth.</hi> Some render it <hi type="italic">perjury</hi>, <note n="124"> <div sID="gen44211" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44211" type="x-p"/> </note> but as <foreign xml:lang="he">אלה</foreign> (ā<hi type="italic">lāh</hi>) signifies also a “curse,” I have no doubt that here he employs it to denote a “curse,” and alludes to those curses which Moses in the law threatens against wicked men and transgressors of the law, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.26.16">Leviticus 26:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.15">Deuteronomy 28:15</reference>.) We know that the earth was cursed on account of the transgression of our first parent, so that it brought forth thorns and thistles instead of fruits. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.17 Bible:Gen.3.18">Genesis 3:17, 18</reference>.) The Lord mitigated this curse, so that, although men were ungrateful and unworthy, still it yielded them food. But when we do not cease to sin, and when we add sin to sin, is it not in the highest degree just that the earth should become barren and unfruitful, in order that we may more clearly perceive this curse, and that it may make a deeper impression on our senses?<div eID="gen44210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44212" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And its inhabitants are made desolate.</hi> I think that <foreign xml:lang="he">אשם</foreign> (ā<hi type="italic">shăm</hi>) here means “to make desolate,” rather than “to forsake;” and this is apparent from the context, on which account I have translated it “are made desolate.” But perhaps it will be thought preferable to take the copulative <foreign xml:lang="he">ו</foreign> (<hi type="italic">vau</hi>) as signifying <hi type="italic">because</hi>, and then the meaning will be, “The earth accursed by God is burnt up, <hi type="italic">because</hi> its inhabitants have acted wickedly.” <note n="125"> <div sID="gen44213" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44213" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen44212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44214" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men left.</hi> The word <foreign xml:lang="he">חרו</foreign> (<hi type="italic">charu</hi>) may be taken metaphorically, and I prefer this view of it, which makes the meaning to be, that those whom the wrath of God has consumed are burned up; because the destruction is compared to a conflagration. When he adds, “that few will be left,” we learn from it that this prediction cannot be explained as relating to the last day of judgment, and that, on the contrary, the Prophet foretells and confirms those desolations which threatened various nations, and that he does so in order that the godly may fear, and may be led to repentance, and may be prepared for enduring all things.<div eID="gen44214" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44209" osisID="Isa.24.6" type="section"/>
entries.0ef5ac801b0e7859df542711ea01412010db60ac: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.7" sID="gen44215" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7.</hi> <hi type="italic">The wine hath failed.</hi> The same subject is continued, and the Prophet threatens chiefly against the Jews the desolation of the land. He gives a long description in order to affect them more deeply, and impress them with a conviction of the judgment of God. Their luxury, intemperance, and feasting, are rapidly surveyed, because amidst so great abundance they proudly disobeyed God. Such ingratitude was not peculiar to the Jews or to that age, but it is universally found that they who enjoy abundance rebel against God, and indulge themselves too freely. On this account the Prophet censures them; as if he had said, “Hitherto you have been plunged in luxuries and pleasures, but the Lord will cause you to lead a very different kind of life.” Isaiah speaks of the future as if it had been present, in order to place it more clearly before their eyes.<div eID="gen44216" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44215" osisID="Isa.24.7" type="section"/>
entries.290809d614fe5f4a7626bb72a336b563fcedd7c5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.9" sID="gen44217" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> <hi type="italic">They shall not drink wine with a song.</hi> To drink wine is not in itself evil, because God has appointed it for the use of man; but here the Prophet describes the banquets of drunkards, which were full of licentiousness, songs, and insolence. Again, because they abused their enjoyment of plenty, he threatens them with want, which men almost bring upon themselves, when by their luxury they turn to a bad use the goodness of God.<div eID="gen44218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44219" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Strong drink shall be bitter.</hi> He adds, that if they drink wine, it will be “bitter” to them; because sorrow commonly deprives men of a relish both for what they eat and for what they drink. The meaning may be thus summed up, “Though they have abundance of wine, yet they will be deprived of the use of it, because they will feel such sorrow as shall take away all relish for it.” “Strong drink shall be <hi type="italic">bitter</hi>;” that is, you shall no longer enjoy those pleasures and delights in which you have hitherto indulged.<div eID="gen44219" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44217" osisID="Isa.24.9" type="section"/>
entries.6f92376914099d53eece0c6a69c6c3e6849011f7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.10" sID="gen44220" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi><hi type="italic"> The city of </hi> <note n="126"> <div sID="gen44222" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44222" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic"> vanity is broken down.</hi> I do not object to viewing this as relating especially to the desolation of Jerusalem. Yet it may be gathered from the context that it applies also to other cities; for shortly afterwards he uses the plural number in summoning the nations to appear before the same tribunal. But as the Prophet had his own countrymen chiefly in view, we may properly consider it to denote Jerusalem, which he calls “the city of vanity,” either because there was no solid virtue in it, or because it was destroyed.<div eID="gen44221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44223" type="x-p"/>The word <foreign xml:lang="he">תהו</foreign> (<hi type="italic">tōhū</hi>) may refer either to the destruction itself, or to their crimes, by which they provoked the wrath of God against them. If it be thought better to refer it to their crimes, it will denote “the city of confusion,” in which nothing is regular or properly arranged; and I approve of this interpretation. Yet it may refer to the punishment; for it declares, in my opinion, the cause of the destruction, and gives up the city to ruin, because justice and good government are banished from it.<div eID="gen44223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44224" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Every house is shut up.</hi> This is a proof of solitude, and the only reason why it is added is, to express the desolation of that city.<div eID="gen44224" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44220" osisID="Isa.24.10" type="section"/>
entries.ce103694cca865e298ee8acd71685168b3976dda: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.11" sID="gen44225" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> <hi type="italic">There is a cry about wine.</hi> He means, that there will be a scarcity of wine; for where want or hunger is found, it is accompanied by unceasing complaints, not only in private, but “in the streets” and public places. He therefore points out those doleful sounds and complaints, but, at the same time, reproves their luxury and intemperance, because they were not satisfied with what was necessary, but greedily swallowed wine, and abandoned themselves to every kind of enjoyment. We must supply the contrast. “Hitherto you have had abundance of wine and of food, and you have taken occasion from it to grow insolent against God; and therefore you will justly be deprived of them, and, instead of your wanton indulgence, wailing and lamentations will be heard in the streets.”<div eID="gen44226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44227" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">All joy is darkened.</hi> The metaphor in this second clause deserves attention; for, as we say that joy brightens when it obtains its object, so the Prophet here says, that “joy is darkened,” because sorrow may be said to be a cloud drawn over it. To <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> is not in itself evil, any more than to drink; and the Prophet does not censure joy simply considered, but excessive and immoderate mirth. When men are merry, they lay no restraint on themselves on account of that dissoluteness or love of disorder (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἀταξίαν</foreign>) which is natural to them. The Jews, having behaved insolently and lived luxuriously, are deservedly threatened with the vengeance of God, because most justly is joy taken from us when we know not how to make a right use of the Lord’s benefits, or to rejoice in him. It thus becomes necessary that he should take away our pleasures and delights, and compel us to sigh and groan.<div eID="gen44227" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44225" osisID="Isa.24.11" type="section"/>
entries.469de85aefec5a13f6983707ff4952661ab78377: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.12" sID="gen44228" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi><hi type="italic"> In the city is left desolation.</hi> By an elegant mode of expression he describes the desolation of Jerusalem or of many other cities. The ornament and perfection of cities consists of men; and therefore, when their inhabitants have been removed, cities are said to be deserted. The Prophet says ironically, that “ruin” will be left; but the word <foreign xml:lang="he">שמה</foreign> (<hi type="italic">shămmăh</hi>) is rendered by others <hi type="italic">desolation</hi>, which amounts to the same thing.<div eID="gen44229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44230" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And the gate is smitten with desolation.</hi> He mentions the <hi type="italic">gates</hi>, because in them the crowded population of the city was seen, for there the people assembled, and there the courts of justice were held. At first, therefore, he mentions the whole city, and next he names one part of it, but for the purpose of setting the matter in a stronger light; for although cities be deprived of their inhabitants, yet some are to be seen in the gates; but if the gates be altogether empty, there must be grievous solitude in the whole city.<div eID="gen44230" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44228" osisID="Isa.24.12" type="section"/>
entries.a69a9a6db7f1e11c25e3b4e7efabecd0de55c381: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.13" sID="gen44231" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44232" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">For it shall be in the midst of the land.</hi> As this statement is inserted between the threatenings and the consolation, the Prophet appears to address the chosen people, and not all the nations indiscriminately; if we do not rather say that he describes the dispersion, by which the Jews were divided, as it were, into many nations. But this being a harsh and forced interpretation, I interpret it as simply meaning that some hope is left to the ruined nations, and certainly this prediction applies strictly to the kingdom of Christ; and therefore we need not wonder that some part of the salvation is also promised to the Gentiles.<div eID="gen44232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44233" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">As the shaking of an olive-tree.</hi> The Prophet has elsewhere used the same metaphor, but it was when he spoke of the Church alone. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.17.5 Bible:Isa.17.6">Isaiah 17:5, 6</reference>.) On that occasion he said that some seed of God would be left, that believers might not think that the Church was utterly ruined; for when “the olives are shaken,” still a few olives are left, and some grapes after the vintage; and in like manner, after the terrible destruction which shall fall upon the Church, a small number of the godly will be left. But now he extends the same promise to other parts of the world, as they were to become partakers of the same grace through Christ. Yet there is still a mixture of threatening; as if he had said, that the earth will be deprived of its inhabitants in exactly the same manner as the trees and vines are stripped of their fruits.<div eID="gen44233" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44231" osisID="Isa.24.13" type="section"/>
entries.5977c6976de3f970c8dcd1b72fa22b9ec6d8299d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.14" sID="gen44234" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14.</hi> <hi type="italic">They shall lift up their voice.</hi> He follows out and increases the consolations which he had briefly sketched; for, having formerly (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.19-Isa.10.22">Isaiah 10:19-22</reference>) said that, out of that vast multitude, a few drops would be left, which would nevertheless overflow the whole world, in like manner he now says, that the small number of the godly, which shall be left out of an abundant vintage, will nevertheless rejoice and utter a voice so loud that it will be heard in the most distant countries. This was done by the preaching of the gospel; for, as to the condition of Judea, it appeared to be entirely ruined by it: the national government was taken away, and they were broken down by foreign and civil wars in such a manner that they never could rise above them. The rest of the world was dumb in singing the praises of God, and deaf to hear his voice; but as the Jews were the first fruits, I shall willingly admit that they are here placed in the highest rank.<div eID="gen44235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44236" type="x-p"/>Hence we obtain a remarkable consolation, that the Lord can in a moment restore his Church, and make it most flourishing; or rather, he can, as it were, create it out of nothing; for even out of death, as we have seen, he brings life. Now, this is contrary to nature and to ordinary custom, that so small a number of persons should lift up their voice, and be heard in distant places; for where there are few persons, there is silence, and where there is a crowd, there is commonly a noise. It is therefore a work of God, which goes beyond the course of nature and the ability of men; for otherwise it would appear as if the Prophet uttered what was contradictory, that when the whole of Judea had been laid waste and the world had been emptied, there would be few or almost none left, and yet that their shouting would be heard everywhere. This is in itself incredible, or rather absurd; but, as we have already said, it is an astonishing work of God.<div eID="gen44236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44237" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">They shall cry aloud from the sea.</hi> By those heralds he means not only those who were the descendants of the Jews according to the flesh, but those who were descended from them by faith. The <hi type="italic">crying aloud</hi> denotes not only cheerful voices, expressive of gladness and joy, but likewise confidence; for they will freely and boldly utter with a loud voice the praises of God. He states, at the same time, that it is right that believers should be employed in extolling God’s perfections and not their own claims to approbation. By <hi type="italic">the sea</hi>, he obviously means distant countries, and those which lay beyond the sea and were unknown to the Jews.<div eID="gen44237" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44234" osisID="Isa.24.14" type="section"/>
entries.5d8d7f57728b7155e6b44e5f97357e5c814cb100: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.15" sID="gen44238" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi><hi type="italic"> Wherefore glorify Jehovah in the valleys. </hi> <note n="127"> <div sID="gen44240" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44240" type="x-p"/> </note> God’s benefits ought to excite us to gratitude, and we testify it by singing his praises. “What return shall we make,” as David says, “for all the benefits which he has bestowed on us, but to take the cup of thanksgiving for salvation, and call on the name of the Lord?” The Prophet therefore observes this order; having spoken of the restoration of the Church, he exhorts us to offer the sacrifice of praise.<div eID="gen44239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44241" type="x-p"/>By <hi type="italic">the valleys</hi>, he means countries that are hidden and, as it were, separated from others; for those which are surrounded by mountains are separated and disjoined by nature. The consequence is, that the inhabitants of valleys are less civilized, because they have fewer opportunities of conversing with each other. The meaning is the same as if the Prophet had said, that there will not be a corner so obscure or retired that the praises of God shall not be heard in it.<div eID="gen44241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44242" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The name of Jehovah the God of Israel.</hi> He uses the expression, “the name of the God of Israel,” in order to intimate that all nations will call upon the true God; for, as all nations have a knowledge of God that is natural to them, so all easily turn aside to superstition and false worship. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.19">Romans 1:19</reference>.) But here he speaks of spreading the true religion through the whole world; and this makes it still more evident that the prophecy relates to the kingdom of Christ, under which true religion has at length penetrated into foreign and heathen nations.<div eID="gen44242" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44238" osisID="Isa.24.15" type="section"/>
entries.30f0a2b1a62ad63648dd764e325e20b9d889572f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.16" sID="gen44243" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> <hi type="italic">From the uttermost part </hi> <note n="128"> <div sID="gen44245" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44245" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic"> of the earth.</hi> This verse contains two statements which have some appearance of being at variance with each other. It begins with a joyful description of the praises of God, and next passes on to complaints and lamentations, in which he bewails the treachery of transgressors, who overturn religion and godliness. So far as relates to praises, we have said that we can neither praise God nor call upon him, till he reveal himself to us, and give a taste of his goodness, that we may entertain hope and confident expectation of life. Hence those sayings of David,<div eID="gen44244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44246" type="x-p"/>“In the grave who shall praise thee, O Lord? <lb/> In death who shall confess to thee?” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.6.5">Psalm 6:5</reference>.)<div eID="gen44246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44247" type="x-p"/>When we feel nothing but the wrath of God, we are dumb to his praises; and therefore when he says that the praises of God will be heard, he means that the gospel will be spread through the whole world; that men may acknowledge God to be their Father, and may thus break forth into his praise. “From the uttermost part” is a phrase that deserves attention; for at that time the praises of God were confined to Judea, and were not heard at a distance; but afterwards they began to resound everywhere.
