(<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.76.1 Bible:Ps.76.2">Psalm 76:1, 2</reference>.)<div eID="gen44247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44248" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Glory to the righteous.</hi> Some consider this to be spoken by all believers, as if the song were, “God is glorified on account of his righteousness.” Others read the two clauses as one, “We have heard that glory is given to the righteous God.” Those who think that the heralds of God’s praises are called “righteous,” bring out a very good sense, but do not attend to the word “Glory,” or at least are constrained to render the word <foreign xml:lang="he">צבי</foreign> (<hi type="italic">tzēbī</hi>) <hi type="italic">joy.</hi> <note n="129"> <div sID="gen44249" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44249" type="x-p"/> </note> He makes use of the preterite, “We have heard,” instead of the future tense; and his reason for doing so is, that he intended to cheer the hearts of the godly by some consolation; “We shall again hear the praises of God;” for this is more than if he had said, “They will be heard.” He speaks also in the first person, in order to include the whole body of the Church, and thus to awaken the attention of the godly.<div eID="gen44248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44250" type="x-p"/>God is called <hi type="italic">righteous</hi>; and we know that this expression frequently occurs in Scripture, but it belongs to him in a different manner from that in which it belongs to men; for men are called “righteous,” on account of the “righteousness” which has been communicated to them; but God, who is the fountain of righteousness, is called “righteous,” on account of what he performs. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.4">Deuteronomy 32:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.7.9 Bible:Ps.11.7">Psalm 7:9; 11:7</reference>.) And that is a proof of this congratulation and thanksgiving, because from the communication of this righteousness we obtain salvation and life; and therefore, wherever the righteousness of God is, it must be followed by praises and thanksgivings.<div eID="gen44250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44251" type="x-p"/>When the Prophet predicted these things, how incredible might they appear to be! for among the Jews alone was the Lord known and praised. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.76.2">Psalm 76:2</reference>.) To them destruction is foretold, and next the publication of the word, and the celebration of the praises of God; but how could these things be done, when the people of God had been destroyed? Hence we may infer that there were few who believed these predictions. But now that those events have taken place, it is our duty to behold with admiration so great a miracle of God, because, when the Jews had been not only broken down, but almost annihilated, still there flashed from them a spark by which the whole world was enlightened, and all who were kindled by it burst forth into a confession of the truth.<div eID="gen44251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44252" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">My leanness. </hi> <note n="130"> <div sID="gen44253" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44253" type="x-p"/> </note> This passage is explained in various ways; for some translate <foreign xml:lang="he"> רזי</foreign><hi type="italic">(rāzī</hi>) <hi type="italic">secret</hi>, and others <hi type="italic">leanness</hi>. Those who translate it <hi type="italic">secret</hi> understand the Prophet to mean that a double secret has been revealed to him, because the Lord has determined to reward the good and to punish the wicked; for when men look only at the outward appearance of things, and see that the wicked succeed to their wish, and that the godly are overwhelmed by afflictions, they are distressed, and doubt whether the affairs of men are governed by the hand of God, or all things happen by chance; and Solomon shews that thoughts of this kind are the seed of ungodliness. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eccl.8.11">Ecclesiastes 8:11</reference>.) On this account the Psalmist also says, that he “entered into the sanctuary of God,” that he might examine the subject in another manner than by human reason. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.73.17">Psalm 73:17</reference>.) If we adopt that interpretation, the meaning will be, “Though it appear as if there were no reward to the righteous, yet I hold this as a secret imparted to me, that it will be well with them; and although the wicked think that they will escape, yet I know that they will not pass unpunished.” But as this ingenuity appears to be too far-fetched, I prefer a more simple interpretation; and, besides, there immediately follows an interjection expressive of lamentation, <foreign xml:lang="he">אוי</foreign>, (ōī,) <hi type="italic">Wo! </hi>so that I do not think that Isaiah speaks here about the righteous or about their reward.<div eID="gen44252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44254" type="x-p"/>Others more correctly explain it <hi type="italic">leanness</hi>; as if he had said, that through grief he shrinks and grows lean; for as the prosperous and flourishing condition of that people might be called “fatness,” so its wretched and distressed condition might be called “leanness.” Here the Prophet stands forth as the representative of the whole race; and when the Lord cuts it down, he justly complains of his “leanness.” This interpretation, I have said, is probable; for when the Prophet saw the people diminishing in numbers, he had good reason for bewailing that diminution. We know that, when the grace of God was very abundantly poured out, the ancient people was greatly diminished, and the posterity of Abraham was almost annihilated.<div eID="gen44254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44255" type="x-p"/>But we must see if the Prophet does not look farther than to the rejection of his nation, so as to bewail the condition of his bowels, when he foresees that the Church will be heavily distressed; for <foreign xml:lang="he">רז</foreign> (<hi type="italic">rāz</hi>,) which some translate <hi type="italic">secret</hi>, may properly be understood to denote the internal part of the body. In this way the exclamation would be, “My bowels, or my entrails, are pained;” for in a pathetic discourse there is no absurdity in supposing that a word is supplied. When the Lord has extended his Church, it appears to be in a flourishing state, and free from all danger; but when its very inwards or bowels, that is, its own members, give it uneasiness, it is grievously tormented. Hypocrites arise, by whom it is more annoyed than by enemies who “are without.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rev.22.15">Revelation 22:15</reference>.)<div eID="gen44255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44256" type="x-p"/>Such is also the import of those groanings, <foreign xml:lang="he">אוי</foreign>, (ōī,) <hi type="italic">wo to</hi> <hi type="italic">me</hi>; and Isaiah, I have no doubt, intended to intimate that the godly should not think that they will be happy in this world, but should believe that they must maintain a continual strife, even when they might imagine that there is nothing to hinder them from enjoying uninterrupted tranquillity and peace. He wishes to express the feeling of poignant grief which torments the Church inwardly, even in her very bowels; and this affliction is the more deeply to be lamented, because it cannot be avoided; for, as some one says, the Church can neither flee from internal and domestic enemies, nor put them to flight. Isaiah can scarcely find terms adequate to express this miserly<div eID="gen44256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44257" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously.</hi> These words abundantly confirm the expositions which have been already given. How heavy this affliction is, and how deeply it ought to be deplored, we ourselves have abundantly experienced, and still experience every day. Whence arose Popery, and all its corruption, but from this internal evil? for it was an imposthume (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἀπόστημα</foreign>) bred in the very bowels of the Church, which sent forth offensive and diseased matter. How comes it also that, when the Church begins to revive, we see doctrine corrupted and discipline overturned not only by the common people, but by those who ought to have given a good example to others? Is it not because the Church is always subject to this evil?<div eID="gen44257" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44243" osisID="Isa.24.16" type="section"/>
entries.8293252366385ce6950d805b8000a851825a2773: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.17" sID="gen44258" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17</hi> <hi type="italic">Fear, and the pit, and the snare.</hi> The Prophet here discourses against the sins of the people. Formerly he declared that not only one nation, but very many and very distant nations, would have abundant grounds of thanksgiving. He now passes to another doctrine; for I think that these words ought to be separated from what goes before, because Isaiah again threatens the wicked, that they may know that amidst the highest prosperity of the Church they will be miserable. For the sake of cherishing their indifference, wicked men are accustomed rashly to apply the promises of God to themselves, though they do not at all belong to them; and therefore the prophets usually mingle threatenings with them. It is also possible that Isaiah delivered this discourse separately from the rest, and on a different occasion; for neither the prophets themselves nor other learned men divided the chapters. We have often seen different subjects joined together, and others divided which ought to have been joined, which was undoubtedly done through ignorance. However that may be, the Prophet returns to the wicked, and threatens against them severe and dreadful judgment.<div eID="gen44259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44260" type="x-p"/>This description of “fear, the pit, and the snare,” is intended to touch the feelings; for if he had said, in a single word, that destruction awaits the wicked, they would not have been greatly moved. But there is room for doubting if he addresses the Jews alone. For my own part, I should not be much inclined to dispute about this matter; but I think it is more probable that these threatenings related also to other nations, and even to the whole world, of which he had formally prophesied.<div eID="gen44260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44261" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">O inhabitant of the earth.</hi> By “the world” we understand those countries which were known to the Jews, as we have already explained. The meaning is, “Thou art pressed by afflictions so diversified, that thou hast no means of escape.” Amos gives a similar description: “He who shall flee through dread of a lion shall meet a bear; and if he go into the house, when he leaneth on a wall, a serpent shall bite him.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Amos.5.19">Amos 5:19</reference>.) Isaiah formerly said that lions would be sent against the Moabites who had escaped from the battle. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.15.9">Isaiah 15:9</reference>.) God has an endless variety of scourges for punishing the wicked. It is as if he had said, “Know that you cannot escape the hand of God; for he has various methods by which he takes vengeance on their crimes, and thus overtakes those who had hoped to escape by a variety of contrivances. He who escapes from the battle shall be tormented with hunger; and when he is freed from hunger, he will meet some other calamity, as if nets had been laid on all sides to ensnare you.”<div eID="gen44261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44262" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For the windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth are shaken.</hi> This argument confirms what had been already said, that it is impossible for them to escape the vengeance of God, who has prepared for it a free course in heaven and in earth, from the utmost height of heaven down to the depths of the earth. Some think that he alludes (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.7.11">Genesis 7:11</reference>) to the deluge; but, in my opinion, the meaning is simpler, that the wrath of God will be revealed above and below; as if he had said, “The Lord will arm heaven and earth to execute his vengeance against men, that wherever they turn their eyes, they may behold nothing but destruction.”<div eID="gen44262" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44258" osisID="Isa.24.17" type="section"/>
entries.882002b31d0cc9ab8e12115297347af14cbb1967: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.19" sID="gen44263" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> <hi type="italic">By breaking down is the earth broken down.</hi> He heightens his description of punishments by using various modes of expression. A little afterwards he will point out the cause of this “shaking,” which is, that men by their sins had drawn down on themselves such destruction. He now declares that this evil is incurable. We have formerly said that the Prophet explains the same thing in various ways, and for the purpose of striking and arousing those minds which are naturally very sluggish; for there is in the flesh a carelessness which produces contempt of God, and we have too much experience of it both in ourselves and in others. In order, therefore, that the prophets might arouse those who were careless and asleep in their vices, they adorn their style; not because they cared about being thought eloquent, but that they might make their hearers more attentive, and sting them to the quick. Hence the allusions of which these verses are full; hence the brilliant metaphors in the style; hence the threatenings and terrors announced in various ways; the object of all is, that careless men may be aroused.<div eID="gen44264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44265" type="x-p"/>Now, this doctrine ought to be limited to the wicked; not because the godly are exempted from those evils, for they are afflicted as well as other men; but because, when the godly betake themselves to God, and rely wholly upon him, they are not shaken in this manner, and remain firm and steadfast against every assault; while wicked men, who despised the judgments of God, and took unbounded liberties in transgression, are terrified and alarmed, and never find rest.<div eID="gen44265" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44263" osisID="Isa.24.19" type="section"/>
entries.714e2d0556a0842b1828920ac48e42eb9eb27be0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.20" sID="gen44266" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi> <hi type="italic">And shall be removed like a tent. </hi>This does not mean that any change will take place in the position of the earth; but these words, as we have already said, must be referred to men; as if he had said, that there would be no kingly power and no regular government. In short, he intended to describe those changes which he had spoken of in the tenth chapter.<div eID="gen44267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44268" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And the transgressions thereof shall be heavy upon it.</hi> When he says that “the earth is laden with its iniquity,” he has very appropriately assigned this reason, that we may understand that God is never angry with men without a cause; for we ourselves are the authors of all the evils which we suffer. God is by nature disposed to kindness, and regards us with a father’s love; and therefore it is our own fault that we are treated with sharpness and severity, and we have no reason to blame him. <note n="131"> <div sID="gen44269" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44269" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen44268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44270" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And it shall fall, and not rise again.</hi> He at length repeats what he briefly stated a little before, that there will be no remedy for those evils. Some think that this relates to the Jews, whose form of government was entirely taken away, so that they were broken down and scattered, and were scarcely reckoned in the rank of men. But I give a more extensive interpretation, that the distresses of the world will be so severe, that it cannot be restored to its original condition. Men always contend against adverse events, and their minds are full of confidence. Having endured calamities, they think that there will be some room for breathing, and their minds are swelled with false hopes, which the Prophet therefore takes away, that they may not in future deceive themselves by unfounded expectation. Yet it ought to be observed, that this general statement does not set aside the exception which Isaiah formerly made.<div eID="gen44270" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44266" osisID="Isa.24.20" type="section"/>
entries.40861f2d04ca380c985bc97c62b2540d4c266fb5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.21" sID="gen44271" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21. </hi><hi type="italic">And it shall come to pass.</hi> This passage has tortured the minds of many commentators, and various interpretations have been offered by various writers. Some think that this relates to the sun and the stars, and others, that it relates to the devils, who will be punished along with the wicked. Others refer it to the Jews, on whom God had bestowed a remarkable privilege. But I cannot adopt any of those interpretations. <note n="132"> <div sID="gen44273" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44273" type="x-p"/> </note> The simple and genuine meaning, therefore, appears to me to be, that no power will be so high as to be exempted from those scourges of God; and though they raise themselves above the clouds, yet the hand of God will reach them; as it is said in the Psalm,<div eID="gen44272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44274" type="x-p"/>“Whither shall I go from thy Spirit? and whither shall I flee from thy face? If I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, there also shall thy hand pursue me.” <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.139.7-Ps.139.10">Psalm 139:7-10</reference>.<div eID="gen44274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44275" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Jehovah will visit upon the army on high.</hi> <note n="133"> <div sID="gen44276" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44276" type="x-p"/> </note> This is a metaphor by which he denotes kings and princes, who shine and sparkle in the world like stars; and he afterwards explains this metaphor in direct language, by adding <hi type="italic">upon the kings of the earth</hi>; for I do not think that they ought to be separated, as if he were speaking of different subjects, but that there is a repetition of the same statement, so that the latter clause explains the former. But perhaps it will be thought preferable to explain it thus: “he will visit on the kingdoms of the earth,” even on those things which appear to surpass the rank of men; for some things rise so much above others, that they appear as if they did not belong to the ordinary rank. The word <hi type="italic">visit</hi> must relate to punishment, as even the context shews plainly enough.<div eID="gen44275" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44271" osisID="Isa.24.21" type="section"/>
entries.83870b498524114736a2e3e3ab72f820bc57d17d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.24.22" sID="gen44277" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22. </hi><hi type="italic">And they shall be gathered together, and shall be shut up in prison.</hi> He continues his subject in the beginning of the verse. The mode of expression is metaphorical; for they were not all captives, but God reduced them to servitude, as if a man held in his hand the enemies whom he subdued. He therefore brings forward God as a conqueror, who shuts up enemies in prison, as captives are commonly shut up. We know that men, as it were, flee from God, and despise him, so long as he spares them, and exercises any forbearance towards them; and on this account also he threatens that they shall be thrown into prison in large masses, that they may not solace themselves with their multitude.<div eID="gen44278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44279" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Afterwards they shall be visited.</hi> When he adds that after a time “they shall be visited,” it is not simply a promise, but includes also a threatening to this effect, “As formerly by their obstinacy they mocked God, and excessively prolonged the time of sinning, so God will punish without making haste, till at length, though late, they acknowledge the cause of their distresses.” Thus earthly judges frequently do not deign to admit into their presence the malefactors who have offended them, but plunge them into darkness and filth, and gradually wear them out, in order to subdue their obstinacy. Again, as there are two ways in which God visits the world, either when he punishes the wicked, or when he shews to the elect the tokens of a Father’s kindness, the word <hi type="italic">visit</hi> here signifies “to look upon;” and thus the Prophet softens the harshness of the threatening. It was necessary that the hearts of the godly should be supported amidst these distresses, that they might not faint; and on their account, therefore, after various threatenings, the prophets are wont to add consolations. As these statements tended to support believers, they were undoubtedly addressed to the Jews, among whom chiefly faith was found, or rather, there was none to be seen anywhere else.<div eID="gen44279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44280" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">After many days.</hi> This also deserves attention. It was intended to try the faith of the godly; <note n="134"> <div sID="gen44281" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44281" type="x-p"/> </note> for we are hasty in our desires, and would wish that God should immediately perform his promises: we complain that he is slow, and we cannot brook any delay. It is therefore our duty to wait patiently for that mercy; and no delay, however long, should make us lose heart. Yet it ought also to be observed, that this does not refer to all; for, as we saw a little before, God had determined to save but a small remnant; and this ought to quicken us the more, that, being humbled by slow and long-continued punishments, we may meet God who visits us.<div eID="gen44280" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.24.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44277" osisID="Isa.24.22" type="section"/>
entries.441401d2f706f6782b8e6d50c0343e40dadf77ef:
23. The moon shall be confounded. Many commentators think that the Prophet waxes still more wroth against the Jews, so far as to say, that the sun and moon and stars are ashamed of their unbelief, and that not only men, but creatures devoid of speech, will abhor them; but this appears to be far removed from the meaning and design of the Prophet. I have no doubt that he continues to give the consolation which he had glanced at in the former verse; “When the Lord shall visit his people, and cleanse the Church from its defilement, he will establish a kingdom so illustrious that it will darken the sun and stars by its brightness.” This mode of expression is frequently employed by the prophets, and we have formerly seen it. Since, therefore, God will establish your kingdom on Mount Zion, so great will be its splendor in the restoration of the people, that those things which dazzle the eyes of men, will be dark in comparison of it; and, for the purpose of expressing this, he has mentioned those objects which surpass all others in brightness.
When the Lord of hosts shall reign in Mount Zion. Some think that the word reign denotes God’s vengeance; but this is inaccurate, for although the Lord is said to reign when he discharges the office of a Judge, yet the complex phrase, “the reign of God in Mount Zion,” always denotes mercy and salvation. He speaks of the restoration of the Church, and hence it follows, that it is only in Christ that those things are fulfilled.
And before his elders glory. By expressly mentioning the “elders,” he employs a figure of speech frequently used in Scripture, by which the chief part of the Church is taken for the whole body of it. And yet it is not without a special design that he denotes, by the term “elders,” not only the priests, but other governors who preside over discipline and morals, and by whose moderation and prudence others ought to be guided. Under their name he includes the whole nation, not only because they represent the whole body, and because the common people are in some measure concealed under their shadow, but likewise that believers may entertain hope of future restoration; for otherwise it would have been of little or no avail that a scattered multitude should be left like a mutilated body or a confused mass. Not without good reason did he use the phrase, “and before his elders,” that the Jews might know that the power of God would be visibly and strikingly displayed; not that it can be perceived by the bodily senses, but by faith. He reigns in such a manner, that we feel that he is present with us; and if we did not comprehend this, it would yield us no consolation.
Glory.
{Bogus footnote}
Instead of “glory” some read “gloriously,” and others, “glorious.” I prefer to take it simply as a substantive, though there is little difference in the meaning. He shews how great will be the splendor and glory of God, when the kingdom of Christ shall be established, because all that is brilliant must be obscured, and the glory of Christ alone must hold a high and prominent place. Hence it follows, that then only does God receive his just rights, and the honor due to him, when all creatures are placed in subjection, and he alone shines before our eyes.
CHAPTER 25
Isaiah Chapter 25:1-12
1. O Lord, thou art my God: I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name: for thou hast done wonderful things; thy counsels of old are faithfulness and truth.
1. Iehova Deus meus es tu; exaltabo te: celebrabor nomin tuum; quia fecisti rem mirificam; consilia iam olim decreta, veritatem firmam.
2. For thou hast made of a city an heap; of a defenced city a ruin: a palace of strangers to be no city; it shall never be built.
2. Quia posuisti ex urbe acervum, urbem munitam in ruinam; palatium extraneorum, ut non sit civitas, nec unquam ædificetur.
3. Therefore shall the strong people glorify thee, the city of the terrible nations shall fear thee.
3. Propterea glorificabit te populus fortis; civitas gentium robustarum timebit te.
4. For thou hast been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall.
4. Nam fuisti fortitudo pauperi; fortitudo, inquam, egeno in afflictione ejus; refugium ab inundatione, umbra ab æstu, quia spiritus fortium (aut, violentorum) quasi turbo (vel, inundatio) contra murum.
5. Thou shalt bring down the noise of strangers, as the heat in a dry place; even the heat with the shadow of a cloud: the branch of the terrible ones shall be brought low.
5. Sicut æstum in arido, strepitum alienorum humiliabis, æstum in umbra nubis; clamorem (vel, cantum, vel, excisionem) fortium humiliabit.
6. And in this mountain shall the Lord of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees; of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined.
6. Et faciet Iehova exercituum cunctis populis in monte isto convivium pinguium, convivium defecatorum; pinguium, inquam, medullatorum; defecatorum liquidorum.
7. And he will destroy in this mountain the face of the covering cast over all people, and the veil that is spread over all nations.
7. Et destruet in monte isto faciem involucri quo involuti sunt populi omnes, et operimentum quad expansum est super omnes gentes.
8. He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord God will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the Lord hath spoken it.
8. Destruxit mortem in æternum. Et absterget Dominus Iehova lachrymam a cunctis faciebus, et opprobrium populi sui auferet ab universa terra; quia Iehova locutus est.
9. And it shall be said in that day, Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the Lord; we have waited for him, we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation.
9. Et dicetur in die illa: Ecce Deus noster iste; expectavimus eum, et salvabit nos. Iste Iehova; expectavimus eum, exultabimus, et lætabimur in salute ejus.
10. For in this mountain shall the hand of the Lord rest, and Moab shall be trodden down under him, even as straw is trodden down for the dunghill.
10. Nam quiescet manus Iehovæ in monte isto; et triturabitur Moab subter eum, sicut trituratur palea in sterquilinio.
11. And he shall spread forth his hands in the midst of them, as he that swimmeth spreadeth forth his hands to swim; and he shall bring down their pride together with the spoils of their hands.
11. Et extendet manum suam sub medio ejus, sicut extendit natator ad natandum; et humiliabit superbiam ejus, cum brachiis manuum suarum.
12. And the fortress of the high fort of thy walls shall he bring down, lay low, and bring to the ground, even to the dust.
12. Et munitionem sublimitatis murorum tuorum sternet, humiliabit, dejiciet in terram, ad pulverem.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="24" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXIV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>BEhold, the LORD maketh the earth<ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>the land,</ns0:hi> to wit, of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Iudaea.</ns0:hi> It is usual with all Writers, when they write of their own Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />try, to call it <ns0:hi>the land,</ns0:hi> by way of eminency. There are many things in this Prophecy which manifestly concern this Land and People; and nothing, at least before <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21. which may be taken as a new and additional Prophecy, which is necessarily to be understood of other Nations. But this I speak with submission, and due respect to those Lear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned and Judicious Interpreters who take this to be a Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phecy against <ns0:hi>Iudaea,</ns0:hi> and all the neighbouring Nations.</ns0:note> empty, and maketh it waste<ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He will shortly make it waste, first by the <ns0:hi>Assyrians,</ns0:hi> and then by the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> pervert<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the face thereof.</ns0:note> turneth it up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />side down<ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Bringeth it into great disorder and confusion.</ns0:note>, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And it shall be, as with the people, so with the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> prince<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Hos. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 9.</ns0:note> priest<ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The approaching Calamity shall be universal, without any respect or distinction of Persons or Ranks of Men; the Priests themselves having been Partakers of the Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples Sins, shall also partake with them in their Plagues.</ns0:note>; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 7. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, 13.</ns0:note> as with the buyer, so with the seller<ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Purchaser of Lands shall have no more left than he who hath sold all his Patrimony; and all Persons shall be made equal in Beggary and Slavery.</ns0:note>; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury; so with the giver of usury to him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 The land shall be utterly emptied, and ut<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terly spoiled: for the LORD hath spoken this word.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 The earth mourneth <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> fadeth away, the world <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">From this Word some infer, That this Prophecy con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerns not onely the Land of <ns0:hi>Iudaea,</ns0:hi> but also the neighbour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Countries: But if the proper Signification of that Word be urged, this Prophecy must be extended to all the Parts of the World, which these Learned men will not allow. And <ns0:hi>the world,</ns0:hi> both in Scripture, and other Authors, is oft used Synechdochically for that which is in truth but a small part of it, at least in comparison with the Whole; as it is not onely of the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Empire, as <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 2. 1. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 11. 28. but also of <ns0:hi>Babylon, Isa.</ns0:hi> 13. 11. and, which cometh nearer to the point, of this very Land of <ns0:hi>Iudaea,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 12. 19. & 18. 20. and elsewhere. And therefore it may well be so understood here, especially when this Word <ns0:hi>world</ns0:hi> is explained by those other Words <ns0:hi>the earth,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>the land,</ns0:hi> which the very next Verse sheweth to be meant of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Iudaea,</ns0:hi> as we shall there discover.</ns0:note> languisheth <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> fadeth away, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the heighth of the people.</ns0:note> the haugh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty people <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Not onely Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon People, who use to be of low Spirits; but the High and Lofty ones, who use to be stout in their Words and Carriages towards me, and to deride my Threatnings.</ns0:note> of the earth do languish.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 3. 17.</ns0:note> The earth also <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>And the land,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>this land;</ns0:hi> for here is an empha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tical Article in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Text.</ns0:note> is defiled under the inha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bitants thereof<ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">By the Wickedness of its People; of which see <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 18. 25, 27, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 35. 33. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: because they have transgressed the laws<ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The Laws of God revealed to them, and pressed upon them in a singular manner, called simply <ns0:hi>the laws,</ns0:hi> as the Word of God is oft-times called <ns0:hi>the word</ns0:hi> by way of emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nency.</ns0:note>, changed the ordinance <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">God's Ordinances concerning his Worship and Service; the Singular being put collectively for the Plural.</ns0:note>, broken the everlasting covenant<ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The Covenant made between God and <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> and all his Posterity, renewed with the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> at <ns0:hi>Sinai,</ns0:hi> which was everlasting, both on God's part, who, upon the Condi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions therein expressed, engaged himself to be a God to them and to their Seed for ever; and on <ns0:hi>Israels</ns0:hi> part, who were obliged thereby to constant and perpetual Obedience through all Generations. All these Clauses clearly prove, that <ns0:hi>the earth</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>land</ns0:hi> which this Prophecy concerns, is no other than the Land of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iudah.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:586" />6 Therefore hath the curse <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Curse of God threatned to Transgressours, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. 15. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and 29. 20. and imprecated by and upon them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves, if they should not persist in their Obedience to God, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 26. and elsewhere.</ns0:note> devoured the earth, and they that dwell therein are desolate: therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Are consum'd by the Wrath of God, which is commonly compared to Fire.</ns0:note>, and few men left.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 16. 8, 9. Joel 1. 10, 12.</ns0:note> The new wine mourneth <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Because there are either none, or none but the Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies of God and <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> to drink it. Grief is ascribed to senceless Creatures by a Figure usual in all Authors.</ns0:note>, the vine lan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guisheth <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther because there are no People left to dress it, or gather its Grapes; or because it is broken down and spoiled by the Enemy.</ns0:note>, all the merry-hearted <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">That made their Hearts merry with Wine, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 104. 15.</ns0:note> do sigh.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 The mirth <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 7. 34. & 16. 9. & 25. 10. Ezek. 26. 13. Hos. 2. 11.</ns0:note> of tabrets <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Which they used in their Feasts and Revellings.</ns0:note> ceaseth, the noise <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The Word properly signifies a roaring Noise and confused Cla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mour, such as drunken men make, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 78. 65. <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 9. 15.</ns0:note> of them that rejoyce endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 They shall not drink wine with a song, strong drink shall be bitter to them that drink it <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Because of the Fears and Miseries wherewith it is mixed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 The city <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and other Cities; for the Singular Word may be here taken collectively.</ns0:note> of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> empti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness.</ns0:note> confusion <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>of vanity,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>empti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>desolation;</ns0:hi> for this <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Word signifies all these things. And the City may be thus called, either, 1. in re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gard of the Judgments of God coming upon it, as if he had said, a City devoted to Desolation or Destruction, to be emptied of its Goods and People: or, 2. for its Sin, a City of Confusion or Disorder, breaking all the Laws and Orders which God had established among them; or a City that <ns0:hi>walketh with</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>after vanity,</ns0:hi> as the Scripture speaks, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 31. 5. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 2. 5. that <ns0:hi>loveth</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>speaketh vanity,</ns0:hi> as they did <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 4. 2. & 12. 2. And this may seem most convenient, that the Sin of the City should be noted in this Word, as the Punishment is expressed in the next.</ns0:note> is broken down: every house is shut up <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Either for fear of the Enemy who have entred the City; or rather, because the Inhabitants are either fled, or dead, or gone in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to Captivity, and so there are none to go into it, or come out of it.</ns0:note>, that no man may come in.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 <ns0:hi>There is</ns0:hi> a crying for wine <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">For the want or loss of their Wine, and spoil of their Vines, whereby they were deprived of the Means both of their Delight and Profit. Whereby he intimates their gross Sensuality and Sottishness, that in stead of crying for their Sins, and humbling themselves under God's Judgments, did onely <ns0:hi>howl for their corn, and wine, and oil,</ns0:hi> as they did <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 7. 14.</ns0:note> in the streets, all joy is darkned, the mirth of the land is gone.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 In the city is left desolation, and the gate is smitten with destruction <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Gates of the City are totally ruined, that the Enemy may enter when and where they please.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 When thus it shall be <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">When this Judgment shall be executed.</ns0:note> in the midst of the land <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">In the Land: But withal this Phrase may intimate, that the Judgment should not be sleight and superficial, and in the Skirts of the Land; but that it should reach their very Heart, their most inward and best defended Parts.</ns0:note> among the people, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 17. 5, 6.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>there shall be</ns0:hi> as the shaking of an olive-tree, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> as the gleaning<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />grapes when the vintage is done <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">There shall be left a Remnant, and that but a very small Rem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nant; as there are some few, and but a few Olives or Grapes left after the Vintage is over. Which, by compa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring this with the following Verse, seems to be added by way of mitigation, to signifie, that God would in Judgment remember Mercy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 They <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The Remnant preserved.</ns0:note> shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the LORD <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">For his glorious Power and Goodness manifested in their Deliverance.</ns0:note>, they shall cry aloud <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">In way of Exultation and Thanksgiving to God.</ns0:note> from the sea <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">From the Isles of the Sea, as this is explained in the next Verse; from those Parts beyond the Sea into which they were carried Captive, and in which they were miraculously preserved.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 Wherefore, glorifie ye the LORD <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">These are the Words either, 1. of the Remnant, who being themselves delivered, do encourage and exhort their Brethren to glorifie God with them: or, 2. of the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet, directing and exciting God's People to glorifie God in their Afflictions, because of that Deliverance which he had promised, and would assuredly give to them.</ns0:note> in the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> valleys.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 39. 6.</ns0:note> fires <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">When you are in the Furnace of Affliction; although this Word is never used in Scripture in this sence. Others therefore render the Word, <ns0:hi>in the valleys;</ns0:hi> and others, <ns0:hi>in the holes,</ns0:hi> you that are now forced to hide your selves in Holes. Possibly it may be better rendred, <ns0:hi>for light</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>illumination;</ns0:hi> which may be understood either of the Light of the Truth which God would reveal to them; or for the Comfort and Felici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty which God would confer upon them; Light being fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently taken both ways in Scripture. For this <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Word, in all other Places of Scripture where it is found, signifies that <ns0:hi>Urim</ns0:hi> which was in the High-Priest's Breast<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plate, and which properly signifies <ns0:hi>illumination,</ns0:hi> as both Jews and Christians render it, whereof that was both a Sign and an Instrument; of which see on <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 28. 30. Add to this, that this part of the Prophecy seems to con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cern the Days of the Gospel, and that Light which the Jews should then receive by the <ns0:hi>Messias,</ns0:hi> of whom the High-Priest with his Ephod and Urim was a Type. And so this is an Exhortation to the converted Jews to bless God for the true Urim, even for Christ and the Gospel. And some of the ancient Translators had this Signification of the Word in their Eye, as the <ns0:hi>Vulgar Latin,</ns0:hi> who render it, <ns0:hi>in doctrines;</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Chaldee,</ns0:hi> who translate it, <ns0:hi>when light shall come to the just.</ns0:hi> But this I propose with submission.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> the Name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">In remote Countries, beyond the Sea, which in Scripture are commonly called <ns0:hi>isles,</ns0:hi> as hath been formerly and oft obser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved. Whereby he seems to imply, that he here speaks not so much of a Temporal Felicity which the Jews should re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive and enjoy in their own Country, as of a Spiritual Ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vantage which they should have by the <ns0:hi>Messias</ns0:hi> in the Places where they were dispersed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 From the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> wing.</ns0:note> uttermost part of the earth <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">From all the Parts of the Earth or Land in which the Jews are or shall be.</ns0:note> have we heard songs <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Songs of Joy and Praise.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> glory to the righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>glory</ns0:hi> be <ns0:hi>to the righteous;</ns0:hi> which may seem to be the Matter of the Song. By <ns0:hi>the righteous</ns0:hi> may be here understood ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, 1. the Generation of Righteous and Holy Men, who formerly were despised, but now, upon this eminent Deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verance, shall be highly honoured: or, 2. the Lord, whom they were exhorted to glorifie in the foregoing Verse, and who may well be called <ns0:hi>the righteous one,</ns0:hi> as he is frequently stiled <ns0:hi>the holy one,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 11. 9. <ns0:hi>Habak.</ns0:hi> 3. 3. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> or, 3. the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> to whom this Title of <ns0:hi>just</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>righteous</ns0:hi> is frequently given, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53. 11. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 23. 5. <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 9. 9. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> And the believing Jews call him <ns0:hi>righteous</ns0:hi> emphatically, partly to in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />timate that he is the Author and Procurer of all true Righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teousness, and partly in opposition to their unbelieving Bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren, who rejected and condemned him as a Malefactor. All which the Prophet foresaw by the Spirit of Prophecy.</ns0:note>: but I said <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">But in the midst of these joyful Tidings, I discern some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing which interrupts my Joys, and gives me cause of bit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter complaint and lamentation.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Lean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness to me. <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> My secret to me.</ns0:note> My leanness, my leanness <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">I saint and pine away for grief, for the following Reason.</ns0:note>, wo unto me: the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The Jews, who have been frequently guilty of great perfidiousness towards God, are now acting the same Part. Which he speaks either, 1. of those who lived in his time; or rather, 2. of those who should live when the <ns0:hi>Messias</ns0:hi> was upon Earth, of whom he foresaw by the Spirit, that they would forsake God, and reject their <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> and thereby bring utter Destruction upon themselves. For even the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Doctors expound this Place of the Perfidiousness of some Jews in the times of the <ns0:hi>Messiah.</ns0:hi> And it is not strange that so sad a sight made the Prophet cry out, <ns0:hi>My leanness, &c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He repeats it, to shew the horridness of the Crime, and how deeply he was affected with it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:586" />17 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 48. 43, 44. See 1 Kin. 19. 17. Amos 5. 19.</ns0:note> Fear, and the pit, and the snare <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Great and various Judgments, some actually inflicted, and others expected and justly feared, as the punishment of their last-mentioned Treachery.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on thee, O inhabitant of the earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And it shall come to pass, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> he who fleeth from the noise of the fear <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Upon the Report of some terrible Evil coming towards him, the Act <ns0:hi>fear,</ns0:hi> being here put for the Object, or the thing feared, as it is in many places. And thus this very Phrase is taken <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 15. 21.</ns0:note>, shall fall into the pit <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">When he designs to avoid one Danger, by so doing he shall plunge himself into ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, and a greater Mischief.</ns0:note>; and he that cometh up out of the midst of the pit, shall be taken in the snare; for the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 7. 11.</ns0:note> win<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dows from on high are open, and the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 18. 7.</ns0:note> foundati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons of the earth do shake <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Both Heaven and Earth conspire against him. He alludes to the Deluge of Waters which God poured down from Heaven, and to the Earth<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quakes which he oft-times causeth below.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 The earth is utterly broken down<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This is repeated again, partly to shew the dreadful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness and certainty of these Judgments, and partly to awa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken and affect the stupid <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> who greatly needed it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 The earth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The People of the Earth.</ns0:note> shall <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 19. 14.</ns0:note> reel to and fro like a drunkard <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Shall be sorely perplex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed and distressed, not knowing whither to go, nor what to do.</ns0:note>, and shall be removed like a cottage <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>like a lodge</ns0:hi> in a Garden, of which this Word is used <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 1. 8. which is soon taken down, and set up in ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther place, as occasion requires.                   <ns0:p n="23">23 Then the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13. 10. Ezek. 32. 7. Joel 2. 31. & 3. 15.</ns0:note> moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>The sun</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>moon</ns0:hi> are here considered either, 1. as they were abused to Idolatry; for these two were most eminent Idols, and most generally worshipped, especially in those Eastern Countries, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 4. 19. & 17. 3. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 31. 26. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and so may be put for all Idols, which were confounded by Christ at his coming, as was foretold in Scripture, and ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rified by the Testimony of Ancient, yea even of Heathen Historians: Or, 2. as they were the most eminent and glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious Lights of the World, and were oft used, both in Scri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pture and other Authors, to signifie the great Kings and Potentates and Glories of the World, as hath been formerly noted, and we shall have further occasion to remember.                         <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> there shall be glory before his an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cients.</ns0:note> before his ancients <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Before his Ministers, who are in some sort the Courtiers of this King of Glory, as being continually attending upon him, and enjoying his Presence, and executing the Powers and Offi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces of his Kingdom; and especially before his Apostles, who were the Witnesses of his Divine Words and Works, and particularly of his Resurrection and Ascension, by which he entred upon his Kingdom; and of the Exercise of his Roy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al Power, in subduing both Jews and Gentiles to himself. The Word <ns0:hi>ancient</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>elder</ns0:hi> is not a Name of Age, but of Of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fice, as it is in very many Texts of Scripture.
